speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, May 16, the debate on the motion of Hon. Sir Henry Drayton (Minister of Finance), that Mr. Speaker do now leave the Chair for the House to go into Committee of Ways and Means, and the proposed amendment thereto of Hon. W. S. Fielding.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the occasion of the Budget speech gives to the House and the country the opportunity to review the state of financial health of the nation. A Budget speech, because of what it may contain, is always of interest at any time; but on an occasion such as the present, when the country has passed through four or five years of war that was a new experience for us; when that war has added greatly to our debt; when it has disturbed our economic conditions as they have never been disturbed before;-a Budget under such circumstances as these, is a matter of interest, and profound interest, to the people of any country, and particularly to the people5 of Canada.
Before I discuss the proposals contained in the Budget delivered by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) the other day, I wish to refer to one or two statements made by my hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) and, I think, by the hon. member for Dundas (Mr. Casselman) in his speech the other evening. These hon. gentlemen directed some criticism against my administration of the Department of Agriculture when I was a member of the Government. Their criticism was that I had failed in my duty to the agricultural people of Canada, in that I had permitted their products to be sold in the markets of the world, to the Allies at prices greatly below their actual value; and they therefore chided me and held me up to reproach because that condition had existed. Well, I bear in mind that my
	, ;
hon. friends supported the policy of that time because it was the policy of the Government of the day and not of the Minister of Agriculture. They supported it in the past, and it is rather a late occasion now on which to rake up criticism of this kind. What were the facts that faced the country under those conditions of war? They were such that there were no free markets -for our products. The Allied countries of Europe, as every one in the House and out of it knows, were buying their requirements through one or two agencies who controlled the shipping on the high seas and absolutely controlled the prices that producers in either Canada or the United States could get for their products. Under those circumstances, therefore, there was no other course for the Government of the day to follow than to make the best arrangements possible with the buyers in Europe; and I am free to confess that, in my opinion, in the great majority of cases the Allied purchasing agents, wielding the power they possessed through unified control in buying, dealt fairly generously with the producers on the North American continent.
I desire now to deal with the Budget statement delivered by the Minister of Finance the other day, and I am bound to say that my hon. friend, in the statement he has presented to the House this year, has fallen far short of the standard he set in his Budget speech of a year ago. At that time his speech was clear and courageous; it contained a note of courage and encouragement to the country. On the present occasion, however; these qualities are entirely lacking. A year ago my hon. friend made this declaration:
The duty to-day is not only to carry on the government of the country without any additions to the debt, but, on the other hand, to promote measures which will reduce the nation's obligations.
Now, that was a sound declaration of policy at that time. It contained two things in particular: First, the view that there should be no increase in the debt, and, second, that steps should be taken to reduce the nation's obligations. But what do we find in the present Budget speech? Do we find that ideal carried out by my hon. friend? Not at all. We find, on the contrary, that our debt has increased by over $100,000,000, and we find, as I shall show presently, absolutely not one word by way of provision for the future as to how we shall care for our heavy commitments that fall due, within the next few years. Now, in this statement my hon. friend

figures out a surplus. One would almost imagine that this Budget was the precursor of an election,-and I am not at all certain but that the Government, in the rather uncertain times that lie ahead of them, are making a.virtue of necessity and have dressed up their Budget proposals so that they will have the finest possible appearance to the country. What does my hon. friend claim? He claims a surplus of $69,000,000, and other hon. gentlemen who sit behind him have played upon this string and have pointed out what a splendid thing it is to have a Government that can produce a surplus of $69,000,000 in a year like this. But how does my hon. friend reach his surplus? He has reached it by charging up to capital expenditure items, and very large items, that should be paid out of ordinary revenue. We are faced with our railway situation, which every one admits is serious. Now, one principle, absolutely, should Ibe laid down in the financing of this enterprise, and that is, that the deficits that occur in operation, and the sums that are necessary to meet interest on fixed charges, should be paid out of income and! not charged up to capital. That is only the position which any ordinary business house would take But does my hon. friend do that? Not at all. We find that the interest on these obligations and the operating deficits have been charged up; and after charging them up my hon. friend arrives at a surplus of $69,000,000. If these charges had been met, as they should have been met, and would have been met by a courageous government, there would have been no surplus, and the facts would have been placed frankly before the people that our income last year did not meet our expenditure.
Have we any hope of improvement for the future? My hon. friend is budgeting this year for a considerable sum of money. He hopes to raise the same revenue that he raised last year, namely, $432,000,000, and he details the items. He speaks of estimated consolidated revenue expenditure $343,000,000-I am giving round figures-estimated capital expenditure $27,000,000; estimated demobilization expenditure $7,000,000-a total of $378,000,000. He sets that down as the amount that should be paid out of current revenue, but he goes on further and he has an item of $50,000,000 for the Canadian Northern railway, $89,000,000 for the Grand Trunk railway, and $26,000,000 for the Grand Trunk Pacific railway. Some of these charges in respect of the railways are of
the nature of capital improvements and therefore could properly (be charged to capital; but many of them-I venture to say half of them although the House has not the detailed information from my hon. friend-are charges to meet interest on investments, or to pay operating deficits; and to that extent the statement is not a sound statement to place before the country. My hon. friend practically makes that admission a little later in his Budget speech, and I submit that his statement of our national finances is not such a statement as should be placed before the people at this time. If there ever was a time in the history of Canada when Parliament and the Government should deal frankly with the country in respect to the question of expenditures and revenues it is now, because only by sustaining the courage and receiving the support of our people throughout the country can we hope to pass through the difficult times that lie ahead of us.
And what is the prospect for the coming year? My hon. friend has estimated a revenue of $135,000,000 from customs against $165,000,000 a year ago, a decrease of $30,000,000. But what are the facts as far as the months of March and April are concerned? The month of March, it is true, was in the last fiscal year, but it gives an indication of what we may expect in the few months that are immediately ahead of us. The customs revenue in March declined over $10,000,000 as against March a year ago and the customs revenue in April last declined over $7,000,000, as compared with April a year ago. There is $7,000,000 gone in one month of the $30,000,000 reduction which my hon. friend has provided for. And the same thing will apply to other sources of revenue. There is bound to be shrinkage in our income, and the Government has made absolutely no provision to meet it. They are going along making extravagant expenditure without any regard for the future; and I am afraid that when we come to the end of the present financial year, my hon. friend will have to come to this House with a deficit unless he can improve his book-keeping methods to a greater extent than he has done in the year that has gone past.
But there is one other criticism I wish to offer my hon. friend: He has made no provision whatever-indeed there is no reference whatever in the Budget speech to the matter-for the needs of the future immediately ahead of us. And what are

speechtext:
Yes, we get a shrug of the shoulders, a cynical smile, and the closure.
My hon. friends opposite are just as careless in the little things as they are in the big things. We had an illustration of that the other evening in this House when my hon. friend the Minister of Railways was dealing with his Estimates, and asking for an increase for rqad supervision by a road department that did not exist in the Department of Railways until a year or two ago. For that department $25,000 was asked a year ago, and $55,000 is required this year, and there is no more need for it than there is for the Minister of Marine to have a battleship. The whole Budget is discouraging. And Sir, it is largely misleading; it is not giving the facts to the country as they should be given. What do the members of the Government have to say in connection with it? The Minister of Trade and Commerce, when he spoke, did not offer to' make any defence of if whatever. When the Minister of Marine spoke, he extolled the virtues of protection, and he told how they were going to win elections in the province of Quebec-that is what largely concerns the Minister of Marine. Then the Minister of Militia spent an hour and a quarter the other day endeavouring to convince the House and the country that Canada is not nearly so war-like as many other

nations in the world, notwithstanding- the fact that the Permanent Fopce to-day is almost 1,500 greater strength than it was the year before the war. And then we had the Prime Minister; I must not forget him. He came to the defence of the Government. What had the country a right to expect from my right hon. friend at this time? It had the right to expect some definite lead, some note of encouragement, some declaration as to the need of public and private economy. It should have had a high sounding note from my right hon. friend. But what did the country get? Well, Sir, we got an exhibition of cheap political vaudeville for over two hours and a half.
Talk about inconsistency! My right hon. friend throws his taunts around very freely and very lightly, and he was good enough to direct some particular attention to the hon. gentlemen "who sit angularly opposite" as he describes them. First of all he said that hon. gentlemen "angularly-opposite"-that is, the Progressives-and the Liberals are in the same boat; the next moment he said that one is protectionist and the other is free trade; and then he described us as "servile tools and minions, a dilapidated annex" of my hon. friends who sit to my right. Finally he completely reversed his position and wound up with the assertion that the Government and those who sit behind him were more low tariff than any other party in the country. A more amazing mass of inconsistencies could scarcely be imagined. And he concluded with this pious declaration, "Let this game cease. It is not doing any credit to the politics of Canada."
Was my right hon. friend doing any credit to the politics of Canada while he . was endeavouring during the past six or seven months to annex a number of hon. gentlemen of the Liberal Opposition who sit on this side of the chamber? My right hon. friend is anxious to get representation in the province of Quebec; I do not blame him for that. But let me ask him and this House in all sincerity: Have the methods which he has followed been any credit to the political life of this country? Perhaps he took his inspiration from my hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) and my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Hocken). Both those hon. gentlemen are supposed to have a peculiar liking for the province of Quebec.
Servile tools and minions! Where was my right bon. friend in 1911 and the party that he thm gave adherence to? In that
year he and his party made an arrangement with the Nationalists of Quebec. Not only that but he and his party financed the Nationalists, their allies. The question of reciprocity was not an issue in Quebec. On what did his allies, whom he and his party financed at that time, make their appeal? Scarcely on grounds that would commend themselves to my hon. friends from Frontenac and West Toronto. It was an attack on the Empire. But my right hon. friend was not backward in seeking the assistance of those who then were willing to "shoot holes in the British flag." It does not lie in his mouth to lecture any one in this House upon political morality.
But let us go a step further. My right hon. friend describes us as a "dilapidated annex of the Liberal party, servile tools and minions." .Were those who sit, as he says, angularly opposite, "servile tools and minions" in 1917, when at their country's call, be their judgment right or wrong, they assisted my right hon. friend and his Government when it was on the brink of ruin and in despair? I should like to know if my right hon. friend considers we were "servile tools and minions" at that time. Let my right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) answer. He knows better. And what about the "dilapidated annex"-where has if been? Where was the "dilapidated annex" in Assiniboia two years ago?

He taunts us with not having moved our platform in this House, but he knows very well why it has not been moved. Two years ago when we sought to introduce an amendment to the amendment on the Budget we could not do so.	My
right hon. friend knows that my hon. friends to the right of me have first claim to speak in the Budget debate. We could not move our amendment two years ago, and my right hon. friend was mighty glad that we could not. At that time he had just gathered a few wavering converts into the fold permanently-my hon. friend from Macdonald (Mr. Henders), my hon. friend from Humboldt (Mr. Lang) and several other hon. gentlemen from Western Canada.

My right hon. friend
did not want our amendment to the amendment moved upon that occasion, for he thought his new converts might be frightened. Then he says, "But why did you not move it on going into Supply?" Does not my right hon. friend recall that two years ago last March my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) moved a tariff amendment on going into Supply? And does he not recall the position the Government took, at that time? I was then supposed to be among the faithful, and I spoke in that debate, my right hon. friend, I think also spoke, at any rate the leader of the Government of that day did; and the position every hon. gentleman on the other side took was that the amendment should be voted down, on the ground that the Budget debate was the place to discuss tariff matters in this House.
I can quite conceive of the pleasure it would give my right hon. friend to have us move an amendment on the tariff when going into Committee of Supply. Immediately he would get up and remind us of the speeches we had made on a former occasion that such an amendment should not be moved, and he would appeal to the loyalty of his supporters to vote our amendment down on the ground that the proper time to move it was when the Budget debate took place.
Now, why is all this suggested now? Why did my right hon. friend make that re-

markable speech the other day? I think he expected it might have some effect on a by-election which is now being contested down in the Maritime Provinces. He knows that his chances in that constituency are very slim indeed, but he hoped that he could influence a number of the electors there who have hitherto given support to him and to his policies to vote against the farmer candidate. On what platform is his candidate running in York-Sunbury at the present time? Does the tariff take a leading place in the discussion? Not according to the best information I get. My right hon. friend's candidate is running on a new -no, I will not say an altogether new, platform; it is an old platform of some of my hon. friends opposite. His candidate is saying privately to the Protestants of the constituency: I do not want any Catholic support; are you going to vote for the man whom the Catholics are voting for?

speechtext:
After all, my right hon. friend did attempt one or two arguments in his speech the other day. He attempted t,o make an argument on the binder twine industry. I believe he quoted from Mr. Lambert, now secretary of the Council of Agriculture. Now, Mr. Lambert, it is true, wrote the article that my right hon. friend quoted, hut that article was written in 1911 during the reciprocity campaign, and when Mr. Lambert was a student fresh from the university and doing literary work of a general character. That was simply a youthful effusion on the part of Mr. Lambert, but my right hon. friend attempts to build a substantial argument upon it. And then he goes on and talks about the binder twine industry, pointing out that twenty-five years ago we had 25 binder twine factories in Canada and now we have only 3. Well, does that prove anything particularly? It is true there was a decline in the number of binder twine factories in Canada, but what about other industries? Take the great agricultural implement industry; in 1881, according to the census figures, there were 234 factories in Canada manufacturing agricultural implements; in 1917 there were 90. Is that what protection has done for the agricultural implement industry in this country? And if my hon. friend from North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) wants some further information, I have it. Take boots and shoes: in 1881, according to the census figures, there were over 4,000 establishments in Canada making boots and shoes; in 1917 there were 185. And take the matter of woollen goods: in 1881 there were 1,994 factories in Canada manufacturing woollen goods; in 1917 there were 80. In 1881 these factories gave employment, according to the census figures, to over 18,000 people; in 1917 they gave employment to
a little over 5,000 people. Is that what protection has done to these industries? When my right hon. friend argues, therefore, that the decline in the binder twine industry in Canada was due to the fact that it had no protection, he cannot offer substantial proof of his statement. But take the case of the Brantford Cordage Company, engaged in the binder twine industry: twenty years ago it had only 60 spindles operating; to-day it has over 700 spindles operating, and its output is over 10,000 tons of binder twine annually. My right hon. friend states that the industry was bonused. Well, has it been bonused? It has not had protection or assistance of any kind for ten years, and in the face of that it is expanding and developing.
My right hon. friend spoke also aboui. the cream separator industry, and he played upon what he referred to as our "working the cream separator all over the country." But, while he may pass these clever remarks across the House he cannot get away from the fact that the cream separator industry in Canada, without protection, has developed and prospered. If the Renfrew Machinery Company can make cream separators and build up their business and expand it as they are expanding it in practically every country where cream separators are used, why cannot my hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) makes his ploughs in the same way? The same elements precisely enter into the manufacture of the plough which enter into the manufacture of the cream separator.
After all, what was there in the speech that was delivered by my right hon. friend? I have said that there was no lead to the country; there was no discussion of the grave problems which face us; it was as barren as the frozen wastes of the Arctic regions so far as constructive statesmanship was concerned. And my hon. friend from Regina (Mr. Cowan), who, I am sorry to see, is not in the chamber, went one better; he applied the terms "duplicity" and "deception" to those who sit in this corner of the chamber-my hon. friend from Regina, who forgets to-day what he said yesterday and will repudiate to-morrow what he said to-day.
We come now to a consideration of the tariff proposals. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance has stated that it is not the intention to have any tariff revision. But is that the case? I will not go over the history of the Government's jockeying with the tariff question or

discuss the position that was taken by the Government two years ago. We know then that the expectation was held out to the country, and particularly to some of my western friends, who are sitting with hon. gentlemen opposite, that this tariff revision would take place, and that we would have a tariff with moderate protection; that we would have a tariff behind the walls of which industry would not be allowed to shelter in ease. Then we had the Tariff Commission journeying throughout this country, and later we had the announcement in the Speech from the Throne, a few months ago, that a measure based upon the Tariff Commission's findings would be brought down to this House. But now the Government comes down with the announcement that there is to be no tariff increase. Is that the case, however? This Budget increases the tariff; in its spirit and essence,it is the most protectionist Budget that has been delivered in this House in twenty years. Not only are duties left at the old levels, but new constructions, new interpretations are introduced in the Customs Act, and we find, for instance, as the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) pointed out, that as regards countries in which there is a depreciated currency, 50 per cent of the value of that currency will be taken for purposes of assessing the duty. On the other hand, we find this condition directed against trade with the United States, that the duty is to be levied on the premium in exchange between the United States and Canada. Further, we have the proposal-I do not know what particular merit there may be in it-that all goods coming to Canada must be marked with the name of the country of origin. That may be a perfectly proper measure to take, but it is quite obvious that it simply places another obstacle in the way of those engaged in trade.
At the present time, the Canadian manufacturer has against the United States manufacturer the protection of the adverse exchange. As regards woollens, which carry a duty, I think, of 30 per cent, what is the actual protection that the Canadian woollen manufacturer enjoys to-day by virtue of trade conditions and the acts of this ' Government? He has his 30 per cent duty; he has 12 per cent discount on his dollar in the United States, which discount acts as a protection to him; he has the rate of duty on that, and he has the import tax levied by virtue of the sales tax which the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton)
fMr. Crerar.]
has increased. Altogether the protection that the Canadian woollen manufacturer enjoys to-day is over 40 per cent as against the United States.

That makes a total of $278,500,000 worth of exports directly from our forests. These are the great natural resources of the country. Let me give the same information as regards minerals:
Asbestos	 $12,600,000
Copper	 13,300,000
Nickel	 9,400,000

That makes a total from our mines of $62,900,000.
Then we have our fisheries, $33,000,000, and furs, $12,200,000. If we total these altogether, we find that we have $945,600,000 worth of exports based on the natural resources of this country as against a total export amounting to
$1,190,000,000. My hon. friend from Simcoe North (Mr. Currie) asked a moment ago: What about manufactures? I will tell him. On textiles, we have had a protective duty of over 30 per cent-yes, going as high at times as 40 per cent during the last forty years. What was the magnificent total contribution that our textile industry, that we have been protecting for forty years in this country, made to the exports of Canada? It was $12,350,000 last year.
-What about rubber goods? They have a protection running over 30 per cent, ahd they have been protected for forty years. They added to our total export trade last year by $10,800,000.
And what about clothing?-clothing that every person in this country, high or low, must have, and a great deal of it, because of the rigours of our climate. We have protected clothing in order to develop a clothing manufacturing industry in this country; and after forty years of protection what did it contribute to the sum total of our export trade last year? Only $8,500,000. These figures prove beyond any question of dispute where the real wealth in this country lies. I say again now what I have said before in this House, that it is the height of economic folly for this country to place these high tariff duties in favour of industries that are not based on the natural resources of Canada.
What protection has the farmer got? What protection has the lumberman got? What protection has the fisherman got? None at all. What value is a protective tariff to the Canadian farmer? My hon. friend the Minister of Finance has spoken about the home market, and that has been dealt with by my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark). I want to point out that we are exporting hundreds of millions of dollars worth of produce from our farms more than we can possibly consume in Canada. Is it not therefore the part of wisdom so to shape the fiscal policy of this country as to give encouragement to industries, like agriculture, to the production of our forest wealth, our mineral wealth, and of the wealth from our seas? That is the sound, sane policy for this country to follow, and I am convinced that before very long this country is going to adopt that policy.
Another defect of a protective tariff is this: I submit that protection, with all its increases, and they have been great, simply facilitates the formation of com-[DOT] bines and mergers in this country. I know that some of my friends opposite may differ with me, but I believe that that is the

inevitable result of the system. One of the crying evils that this country has suffered from in the last twenty years has been the exploitation of the Canadian people by stock watering and stock promoting in practically every industry in Canada. Let me give the House a few illustrations-and I could multiply these by a score if it were necessary.
Take the boot and shoe business-an article of vital necessity to the whole Canadian people, because even if we were disposed to do so, the rigours of our climate would not permit us to go barefooted or lightly shod. We find that in 1911 there was a merger of shoe manufacturing concerns in Canada. In that year the Ames-Holden-McCready Company, Limited, was formed, absorbing Ames-Holden, Limited, and the James McCready Company, Limited. The capital issues of these two concerns-capital stock and bonds- amounted to $3,500,000. That was their actual worth as disclosed by their bonds and capital stock. What was that turned into? $3,500,000 of common stock, $2,500,000 of preferred stock, and $1,000,000 of bonds, or a total issue of $7,000,000. One cannot speak with definite knowledge, because one has not access to the records of this company, but I believe that I am not beyond the mark when I make the statement that practically every dollar of that common stock was water. What has been the result? Boots and shoes that y.ou and I, Mr. Speaker, and every one else in this country wear have enioyed a tariff protection of 30 per cent. Where has the value of the common stock of the Ames-Holden-McCready Company gone? In 1920 it sold as high as $137 a share. Is that protecting industry, or is it, as I stated in this House on one occasion before, protecting exploitation of the people?
Take another article which is very commonly used in this country-glass. In 1913 the Dominion Glass Company was formed. What did it embrace? We find that it absorbed the Diamond Glass Company, with $1,000,000 of securities, capital stock and bonds; the Sydenham Glass Company with $300,000, and the Canadian Glass Company with $100,000, or a total capitalization-capital and bonds-of $1,400,000. What happened when the merger was formed? What happened under the alchemy of the stock promoter's wand? The new company that was formed was capitalized as follows:	common stock,
$4,250,000; preferred stock, $2,600,000; bonds, $2,000,000; or a total of $8,850,000. You will say that that common stock had

no value. True, it had no value, then. There was even an inflated value given to the bonds and preferred stock, according to the statement. But what has since happened to the common stock? Under a protection of 32i per cent this company has gone on making its glass bottles, glass jars and other glass products, until the common stock in 1920 sold as high as $69.25 a share. I ask again, is that protecting a legitimate industry in Canada, or is it enabling these promoters, through this protective tariff, to exploit the Canadian people?
I am sorry the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne) is going out because the next example I was going to give was the Sherwin-Williams Paint Company of Canada, Limited. This company according to the records was incorporated in 1911.

There is $4,000,000 of common stock, which in 1911 sold at less than $30 a share; the lowest point the stock touched last year was $75 a share, and all the time there has been a protective tariff on paint coming into this country of over 30 per cent.
I have been represented as being opposed to industries in this country. I am not opposed to industries in Canada. I should like to see industries developed in Canada, but I am opposed, as I trust I shall ever be, to a system of protection that permits this sort of thing and exploits the great masses of the Canadian people in order that a few individuals may enrich themselves.
Now, Sir, the effect of these taxes which my hon. friend the Minister of Finance has imposed is to increase the cost of living in this country; they can have no Other effect. I have shown, as my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) and other hon. gentlemen who have preceded me have shown, that -the purpose of these taxes is to increase the tariff. The operation of the sales tax will also bear heavily upon the poor man. My hon. friend from Red Deer stated the thing in a nutshell in his argument the other day, and so far there has not been an hon. gentleman opposite who has attempted to reply to the argument which my hon. friend advanced. As the hon. member for Red Deer said, the operation of these taxes will raise the prices of commodities in the country. If it raises the prices of commodities it limits and decreases the consumption of them. If it limits and decreases consumption it decreases production, and if it decreases production it brings stagnation to business and unemployment to labour.
That is the inevitable effect of the operation of these taxes. My hon. friend from Red Deer pointed it our clearly, and so far he has not been answered by any hon. gentleman who has attempted to discuss the matter on the other side of the chamber. Furthermore, these taxes are not levied according to the ability of the citizen to pay. Now, I have every sympathy with the position in which the Minister of Finance finds himself, because it is extremely difficult to get the revenues which this country requires in the days we are passing through. But the minister, through the operation of the sales tax, is increasing the cost of living to every person in the country. What about the wealthy man who spends six months in California or Florida, or Europe? He has not to pay taxes on purchases when he is away. But the poor man with the limited income,-he may be out of work, without any income at all, just living on the slender resources he may have accumulated in the past-finds himself in an altogether different situation. What position is he in? and what position is the returned soldier in? This tax will hit them every day in the year; they cannot escape from it; and to that extent my hon. friend has been very unwise in the taxes he is imposing.

I hope the fear is unwarranted, hut I am afraid that my hon. friend, when the year comes to a close, will find that his revenues have not come up to his anticipations. I would urge again upon him and upon the Gevern-ment the great need of .laying down some definite financial policy. I know that the matter of taxes is a difficult one; no one likes to pay taxes. But we must have the revenues that- are required to pay the interest on our debt, to meet the charges for returned soldiers, to pay pensions, maintenance, etc., and to provide for all the other services which are necessary in the public welfare. But we should aim to raise these taxes where they will bear as lightly as possible upon the great mass of the common people of the country, and in that respect I would offer one or two suggestions to the Minister of Finance. I have not very much hope that he will accept them, but nevertheless I proffer them. I think that the income tax might very well have been extended. A man with an income of $20,000 in Canada to-day pays a tax of some $1,500 or $1,600, as compared with a similar tax on a similar income in Great Britain of almost $6,000. It is true that on the larger incomes, running up to $100,000, $150,000 and $200,000, our tax in Canada is heavier than in Great Britain. But I think the range of income might have been extended. I think also that my hon. friend might have somewhat increased the income tax on corporations. He has abolished the business profits tax, and in that respect he has acted wisely. But it does seem to me that the income tax on corporations might have been somewhat, possibly, considerably extended. And then there is another source of revenue that may not be very well understood in the House, although it is one which I think the Government might well consider when it is looking for money with which to carry on public affairs. My hon. friend from Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon) last evening referred to the possibility of raising revenue by a tax on the values of land. The hon. Minister of Marine (Mr. Ballantyne) referred to this subject in his speech the other day, but he spoke of the tax as a land tax, and I desire to draw the distinction clearly between a land tax and a tax on the unimproved values of land, which is a totally different thing from a flat tax on land. How does this tax on the unimproved values of land operate? Let me illustrate it. I know of a case, which has come under my observation, where a certain gentleman in one of the cities of Canada owns an apartment block. He has 
alongside it a vacant lot. He derives his income mainly from the revenues he receives from the dwellings and buildings he rents. He spends very little of his time in Canada, but his agent comes around every month to collect the rents. The vacant lot he holds is increasing in value every year by virtue of the fact that the people around are busy working and carrying on all the activities of a civilized community. What does this gentleman hope to do? What has he done in countless cases in the past? He has reaped the advantage of the increase in value, but he gets off with a very slight, a nominal tax on the land he has held out of use. Now, this tax on the unimproved values of land would have the effect of bringing such land as this into use. It would take for the state simply the increment that comes to the land as a result of the activities of the people living in the community and would be no injustice to anyone; and it would lessen the burden on the poor individual-the workingman, the clerk in the store, the clerk in the law office-who has to pay, in many of our Canadian cities, exorbitant rents in order to get a place in which to live. That is the effect of this. I would suggest to my right hon. friend that this avenue of taxation might well be inquired into. I know that, particularly, in the western provinces, this principle has been applied by the Provincial Governments, and it may be that that field of taxation should be left to them, but it is worth seriously enquiring into. In that connection I have another suggestion to make to my hon. friend and it is this-it mighf be well to-day to have a conference, not only with the provinces but with representatives from some of our larger cities, with a view of reaching some definite understanding as to the relative fields of taxation in Canada.
Now, Sir, I have taken more time than I intended.

Our trade is shrinking, it is shrinking seriously. The effect of the United States tariff legislation has already been alluded bo, and I cannot help but regret the action of my hon. friends opposite when they rejected the reciprocity arrangement of 1911. We have had for several years past one of the best markets for our natural products in the United States. I do not know that we can complain of tfie action they are taking in that country, but I would offer this suggestion to the Minister of Trade and Commerce-

that he might very well say to our friends at Washington " Let us talk this matter over." Let him tell them frankly that we are ready to trade with them on the basis of the 1911 arrangement. That arrangement still stands on their statute books, and it may be that they would yet accept it; and if my hon. friend will do that he will render to Canada one of the best services he has ever given to it in his long and distinguished career.
But I want to point out to my manufacturing friends what the effect is going to be of a restricted market for our agricultural products. We sold last year almost $160,000,000 of agricultural products ,in the United States, and we know the condition that the European markets are in in this respect. Therefore I say to my manufacturing friends, " Where are you going to sell your goods if the Canadian farmer is not prosperous?" It is one of. the unfortunate facts-perhaps it was unavoidable-of a protective tariff that our manufacturing industries have not extended their markets in the world. I have proven that by the figures I quoted to the House. We are at the present time having a decline in the values of farm products. Why, Sir, in the past year alone the value of live animals in Canada has decreased over $350,000,000. The farmers are selling oats for 19 cents a bushel and hides for one cent a pound, as my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) pointed out, and paying $10 and $12 a pair for shoes. You cannot have prosperity in a country under those conditions; and if my manufacturing friends desire to extend their business it should be of the first and greatest concern to them that the farmers of this country are prosperous and remain prosperous.
I would offer this suggestion to the Government also, and to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance with whom I sympathize in his many troubles and tribulations; that we should have a policy of rigid economy absolutely; rigid economy first, last and all the time; rigid economy for five years at any rate until we have refunded our maturing obligations, until we have passed through this period of depression that we are in now and of which we have not yet reached the bottom. Under such circumstances only economy of the most rigid kind can satisfy the demands and needs of the hour.
Then I would offer another suggestion- that we could dispense with expenditures of a local character. Very often in this House we are called upon to vote moneys
221J
for purely local purposes. That is not sound business nor is it sound policy. Local needs should be cared for by local taxation, and that matter is one that could well engage the attention of the Government.
I think also-as I suggested a moment ago-that the Minister of Finance might well call into consultation the treasurers of the various provinces and the treasurers of our large cities-follow the practice that was adopted early in the war when the late Minister of Finance laid down certain restrictions with respect to the sale of securities, and when there was an effort made to unify and co-ordinate the financial policy of Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific. My hon. friend should do that and he should do it without delay, because the burden of taxation upon the people is growing every day and their ability to pay is growing less every day.
I would offer another suggestion to the Government: They might very well discontinue the expenditure on roads and on the housing problem that we have been engaging in for the last few years. That was undertaken at a time when there was apparently a growing need in the country for such purposes, but I submit again that that is expenditure that should be cared for by the provinces or by the municipalities interested. After all, the burdens of the municipalities in Canada and the burdens of the provinces are infinitely less, financially, than are the burdens on the Federal Treasury.
I am not very sanguine that my suggestions will be taken by the Government, but I repeat that our situation is serious- if I cannot impress that upon the Government I hope I may, in some degree, impress it upon the country. The people of Canada to-day-on information given * me a short time ago by a gentleman who I think is usually careful in his estimates- are paying in taxes for federal, provincial [DOT]and municipal purposes over one thousand million dollars a year, and we are paying, to meet our obligations abroad, almost $250,000,000 a year. That burden is a very heavy burden.
Sir, the Government should give some lead to the country. But do we get any lead from the Government either in economy or any other direction at the present time? So far we have not had it. My hon. friends apposite-and I do not wish to do any injustice to them; I think I will be given credit by most hon. gentlemen in this House for fairness-it does seem to me that my hon. friends opposite

are mainly concerned with their political success rather than with the pressing needs of the country at this time, and such a policy can bring no useful result to the Canadian people. There is no doubt, Sir, that our difficulties are great, our problems are serious. I would like to see the Prime Minister-and I do not wish him any ill- I would like to see him, and I would like to see this Government, give a definite lead to the country at the present time, give a definite lead in economy, place frankly before the country the difficulties and the serious nature of the problems that lie immediately ahead of us; and I have faith and confidence in the Canadian people that they will rally to the support of any Government that attempts to meet the necessities of the hour as they should be met. But, Sir, when we look at the Treasury Benches of to-day, when we analyse and study the policy of the Government, when we see the motives that animate it in its public administration of this country's affairs, it offers but little hope for the future. We can only get relief from this condition of affairs when we have had an election, and when the country has had an opportunity to pronounce upon these problems and to elect representatives to this Parliament who will give the Government of this country the efficiency, the vigour, and the courage that it calls for at the present time.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think it is quite six o'clock. I think I will be able to give the hon. gentleman who made that interjection a few facts before six o'clock is reached.
Before entering upon a reply to my hon. friend who has just taken his seat I wish to make one or two remarks with regard to the Budget that has been brought down. I hope that my hon. friend from Marquette, to whom I have listened very patiently, will be on hand when I have to address certain remarks to himself in reply to certain references he has made with regard to the manufacturers. I just throw that out as a hint to my hon. friend, who is now leaving the chamber, in order that he may kindly return if possible. The Budget, as prepared and presented by the Minister of Finance, I consider is upon the whole one of the best and most pleasing that Canada has had in many years. That may be considered

quite a statement for me to make, but we must remember that we are living in very extraordinary times, and therefore we have to fit our views to suit the situation in which we find ourselves placed. That the Minister of Finance should be able to show that we have taken care of all our ordinary expenditure and have a surplus at our command of about $70,000,000 is, I think, an achievement in these days that very few countries can show. The Minister of Finance and I have not seen eye to eye upon every matter of taxation, and it is not to be supposed that we would always agree on such matters. Taxation is never pleasant, and it touches a man in a very sensitive part of his constitution; therefore we must make allowances when we feel that we are taxed severely, knowing that the needs of the treasury are great and must be met regardless of who may be touched and what interests may be affected. I am free to say that I, for one, have felt the taxation very severely. Probably some of my hon. friends opposite will say I did not show it, and I tried not to. I must say, however, that I have been taxed during the past two years in a way that I never expected to live to see; and while my hon. friend from Marquette shouts for more income tax, I do not know where he expects to get very much more than is being collected to-day. I say it, and with some knowledge of the facts, Mr. Speaker, that we have been taxed already to a degree that is affecting our commercial affairs in a very serious way. There is not a bit of doubt about that. All the money that is taken from the pockets of the manufacturer, the merchant or the tradesman is diverted from its ordinary avocation of building up and extending industries, of maintaining those that are here, and of seeing that the workmen are employed. Whenever the money is diverted from the pockets of those who think that they have made it honestly and is put into the Treasury, that money for the time being, is withdrawn from all productive effort; that has been the case to a very large extent in Canada; and I trust that as soon as the Minister of Finance is able to reduce that taxation he will do so. In the meantime we must pay it with the best grace possible, and I for one am endeavouring to do that.
The business profits tax, I am thankful to know, is gone. Probably it was more damaging and dangerous to industry than is the income tax, because the money thus

collected was primarily intended for extensions of factories, for the implanting of new industries, and for all that variety of enterprises to which spare capital can he devoted.
The railway situation, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Marquette, is very serious for the country, and has called for a large portion of our revenue to go into channels for which it was not intended.
And now having made these very brief references to the Budget as a whole, I purpose in the brief time at my disposal to devote considerable attention to the august aggregation of Agrarians sitting across the chamber. I regret that in spite of my reference to 'the hon. member for Marquette he has withdrawn. His speech, as I understand it, was a political speech from start to finish. It was such a speech as probably he has been delivering in New Brunswick recently. It is evidently intended for campaign purposes. The part of his speech that was not devoted to denouncing industry because it was unsuccessful was devoted to opposing those who have made money out of manufacturing. So whether manufacturing was a failure or a success it was just as heartily cursed by the hon. member for Marquette.
I cannot conceive what has imbued apparently so fair-minded a man as the hon. gentleman who leads the Agrarian party to take such a hostile attitude towards all those who are engaged in the industries of this country. He is not attacking merely the few at the head of our industries, he is attacking the bread and butter of every workingman in Canada; and if he succeeds in destroying the industries of this country, as he is evidently bent upon, he is going to throw out of work tens of thousands of workmen from coast to coast. Anybody can see that; everybody knows it. If it were only the three or four or five thousand manufacturers who get the advantage of the protective tariff I would say at once: The number of them does not justify the tariff; take it off. But when you speak of a factory you not only speak of the men at the head of it, of the board of directors, and of the shareholders, but you speak of every man who is at the bench and getting his daily bread by honest toil. I say, Mr. Speaker, that the production of the factory in honest goods is entitled to just as fair consideration, and no fairer, as the production of the field-a statement that cannot be successfully contradicted by any man in this House or outside of it. The honest
toil of the workman that goes into the manufactured product and is sold in the markets of the world or in the home market is just as worthy as the toil that goes into the production of a bushel of wheat or oats or a pound of butter. I stand for both. I have always advocated the policy of helping the farm as well as the factory, and I must say that the feeling evinced by our friends in the West is not at all the same as that which prevails in my county. We have cordial co-operation there between the farmers and the manufacturers. Many of the former quit their farms in the winter time and come and work in our factories, leaving a boy, and in some cases a woman to do the chores, thus allowing the man to earn money during the winter season. That is done throughout Ontario in scores of our cities and towns; and surely that is an advantage that should not be forgotten by the farmer himself. Then take the home market. In the city of Brantford alone we consume more of certain lines of farm products than are grown in the county of Brant. Is that no advantage to the farmer? My hon. friend from Marquette bemoans that we cannot send more agricultural products to the markets of the world. He neglected throughout his entire speech to show, as he very well could, that upwards of seventy-five per cent of the agricultural products of Canada are consumed at home. Is that not worth while? Are you going to sacrifice three-quarters of your market for the sake of a doubtful one-quarter in foreign countries? And still that is the policy proposed by the hon. member for Marquette. He has got another guess coming before he is a statesman big enough to govern a country like Canada, if the speech we have heard this afternoon is to be taken as a measure of his statesmanship. He has shown no breadth of vision. He denounced manufacturing and all those engaged in it; apparently he has no good word for anybody not engaged in agriculture. I do not know that he himself follows agriculture very much. Perhaps he does, but I must say he does not look as though he had been working at it lately.
I stand just as four-square for agriculture and the farmer as for manufacturing and the manufacturer. I have shown that in this House on previous occasions, and there have been times in my political career when I have taken off my coat and helped farmer candidates in my own riding. Although three-quarters of the voters lived in the city, we nominated the farmer and got behind him and did our best to elect him.

I will do that again on any occasion when a farmer runs as a citizen. I say he should run as a citizen of Canada, not as a farmer; we shall never get anywhere by class legislation. The workingman is entitled to a seat in this House. I say, all honour to the workingman who can be elected, and where a workingman will run in one of our towns or cities I am prepared to support him if he runs as a citizen of Canada and not as a nominee of Labour. If a manufacturer runs as nominated by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and is backed only by that organization When he is put into the field, I will absolutely refuse to aid him in any way no matter what his views are. A,m I not consistent? I have never been put in the field by the manufacturers. I have never sought anything from the Manufacturers' Association; I have never been a member of it and do not suppose I ever will be. Any nominations I have ever had have come more from the workingmen than any one else, and I have had the farmers' support as well; in fact, I received more support from that direction In the last election than I did on any previous occasion. I mentiqn this, Mr. Speaker, only to show that I am prepared in all respects to see that our farmer and rural population get their fair representation in this House. As a result of the elections in 1917, if I remember rightly, we had fifty farmers sitting on this side, all elected not as farmers but as citizens of Canada. Are they not farmers still? Are they not good men upon the land? Are they any less men and citizens of Canada because they did not run particularly in the Agrarian interests? I cannot see it, Mr. Speaker. I say, all honour to these men who have been elected in that way as citizens of Canada, who have taken a broad view of the country's affairs, and who have been of the opinion that this country is too large and too varied in its character to be run in any one particular groove. It seems to me, Sir, that that is sound policy.
The member for Marquette uttered a wail of woe with regard to what the manufacturers have done and are doing. But I do not think he can show that the manufacturers have been unduly grasping, or that they have not been managing their businesses fairly well. I read in a pamphlet containing facts with regard to Canada, just issued)-1921-on the second pagfe, that Canada's agricultural wealth in 1919 was estimated at $7,379,299,000, made up as follows:	agricultural production,
(Mr. Cockshutt.]
$1,975,841,000; value of farm land, $2,792,299,000; buildings, $927,548,000; implements, $387,079,000; farm five stock, $1,296,602,000. You will note that the agricultural production was $1,975,841,000 in 1919. Now, let me draw the attention of my hon. friends opposite to what manufacturing did in the year previous to that, 1918-because for some reason or other the book is not as up-to-date in the matter of manufacturing as it is in its figures with regard to agriculture. I read from page 42, which gives figures of the industrial census. The capitalization of industries in 1915 was $1,994,103,272 and in 1918, three years later, it had risen to $3,034,301,915.
