speechtext: We are not talking about munitions; we are talking about products, and there are the figures set forth in a disinterested book, taken from statistics. My hon. friend may twist them as he likes, but the facts are there, and he does not like them. This country is at least half industrial td'-day, and in spite of all the efforts of my agrarian friends they are never going to make Canada a purely agrarian country. Canada is not built on those fines.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is the increase not accounted for by the large increase of prices of manufactured goods? Prices went up 100 per cent in the last five years.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I admit that, but my hon. friend will also admit that the prices of agricultural products advanced as fast as, if not a little faster than, the prices of manufactured goods.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And they are going down a good deal faster than is the case with the agricultural implements.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, we swallow
more of them, I suppose, in our daily round. My hon. friend cannot make any argument with regard to the prices of these articles. The years to which I have referred are both war years, and the prices of all these things were war prices. My

hon. friend is a farmer, and he will know that during the war when the manufacturer was denounced for his high prices the farmer could drive in to his neighbouring town or city in the west, and in exchange for the value of a load of produce of any kind take home more goods than he could ever have taken home in prewar days. That is a statement that cannot be refuted. Of course, I am speaking now of the war time, not of present conditions, because, as the hon. gentleman has pointed out, prices have dropped, and it may be that the agriculturist has suffered more than those engaged in some lines of industry. But if my hon. friends think that the making of goods is all "pie", I advise them to try it. There is the proof of the pudding. They are large sellers of all kinds of goods; I would advise them to try it. They have read some astounding figures with regard to the paint industry and other industries to show that money was being made too fast. The hon. gentleman also read a number of statistics in order to show that some of these industries were making money too slowly and were no good because they could not export to foreign countries. But I have shown, Mr. Speaker, that the industries of Canada produced in 1918 upwards of $3,000,000,000 worth of goods.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will my hon. friend give the figures for 1920?

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am sorry that I cannot do so; as I have said, the book gives the figures in respect to manufacturing only up to 1918 and of agriculture only up to 1919. Of course, the figures for 1920 are not yet available, in any case.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is it not possible that in the figures my hon. friend has given, wheat which has been ground and manufactured into flour is counted in with total manufactures?

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This classification
is not mine; it is prepared by the authority who has prepared it annually in Toronto for many years, Mr. Frank Yeigh. I should say that what he called manufactured goods are manufactured goods, and it is not unlikely that some of them are the product of the farms. But the more we can manufacture in Canada of all these goods; the more we can send out in highly finished form, the more money we in Canada get for them. That is evident, I think, to all.
I noted the other evening the speech of my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle (Mr. Thomson). Apparently he foreshadowed to some extent what we might expect from the leader of the Agrarian party. He made a very vicious attack upon manufacturers and their products. He denounced us as practically eating up the people, and as bQnused, I think he said, to the extent of five or six hundred million dollars-a hundred million dollars did not matter very much. All the same, I think I can show that we have given fairly good results for the money.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle, who, I understand, is chief whip of the Agrarian party, bemoaned very seriously the low price of hides, and I think that bemoaning of his has been echoed by several gentlemen in the Agrarian party. I was thinking of making this suggestion to the Agrarian party, that they take advantage of the low price of hides to lay in one or two new whips for the party. How would that be? I think the hon, member for Qu'Appelle saw that this was coming because he bemoaned the price of hides. Two or three good raw hides could be laid in very cheaply, and I am not sure that they would not have more effect than the hon. member for Qu'Appelle has upon the party at times, because I notice that he has not been able to hold them in subjection at all times during the present session.' Sometimes they voted on one side and sometimes on the other. I commend them for that, but that does not look like good whipping, does it? My hon. friend, when he bemoans all this, should realize that the manufacturers, as well as the farmers, have their troubles. I am not sure that the hon. member for Qu'Appelle is either a farmer or a lawyer. Sometimes, I think he applies legal knowledge to his farming, and sometimes I think he applies his farming knowledge to the. legal profession. He seems to he in a general state of mixture.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And a good one.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is a good one,
is it? There may be differences of opinion qs to that. I very much regret that the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) has not yet come back into the chamber. I got up largely to refute statements that have been made freely by the Agrarian party, not only in this Houses but on the platform throughout the country. I always try to have my statements as nearly as possible correct on the subject on which I am speaking. If I make a mistake, that

mistake has been made unintentionally and not by device. The hon. member for 1 Qu'Appelle the other night repeated a statement made in this House some six or eight weeks ago, when the Minister of Militia and Defence (Mr. Guthrie) was giving to the House certain facts with regard to protection to industries, and particularly with regard to the implement business. The shout came back from across the way-and I think my few friends who remain in the chamber will recognize this -that the reason the United Farmer does not buy his implements in Canada, is because the manufacturer will not sell to him. I think my hon. friend recognizes this statement as having been made.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Certainly.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member
for Qu'Appelle says that, inasmuch as this statement was not contradicted in the House, he takes it for granted that it is correct. Well, if every part of my hon. friend's speech that was not correct was contradicted, there would not be very much left. The reason why we did not contradict this at the time is because it is against the rules of this House to jump up and butt in on a speaker when he is making, no matter how ridiculous, a statement. The statement that he made is one that cannot be borne out by the facts.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Does my hon.
friend deny, that the manufacturers of Canada refused to sell agricultural implements to the Grain Growers of the West when they first wanted to buy them?

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend puts in "when they first wanted to buy them." This statement was made this week in the House, and it has been made several times during this session. I want to say a few words in regard to the matter. When the debate took place in this House about six weeks*ago, in which debate the Minister of Militia and Defence took part, the cry came back-and it was distinctly heard on this side

from several hon. members that the reason why the United Farmers did not buy their implements in Canada was because they could not buy them from Canadian manufacturers. That was a statement, not of the past, but of the present. I have had an opportunity, during the interval, to find out a little about that, and I say to the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Reid), who is an honourable man, that the statement is not correct. These gentlemen, as soon as they made the statement, set about to prove it, but a wise man would have proved the fact
[Mr. Cocksliutt.J
first and made the statement afterwards. That was not the case with the Agrarian party; they rushed in and then they tried to get the facts to back them up in what they hoped was so. It was only two or three days after that statement was made in the House that their friend, Mr. Rice Jones, whose name, I think my hon. friends will realize, is a comparatively well-known name in the West, wired to a certain firm in Brantford to know if he could be received by that firm on business. The answer went back promptly naming a day and asking him to come on.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They will all sell now.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He did not come; but he wired again in a few days to know if he could be received, and again he got an answer:	" Come on." Apparently, he
was looking for a telegram to say:	"We
will not meet you and we will not sell to you;" but he did not get it. He got an invitation to come on, and that is the last thing that he wanted. But finally, after great deliberation, and no doubt after some of my hon. friends had been consulted, he came on and the firm on whom he waited said to him:	"Submit your proposition
with regard to buying implements; we will consider it, and we hope to do business." But up to the last time that I have heard, not a word has come out from the hon. gentleman's friend in the West since. Does that show any strong desire to buy in Ontario? He wanted to be refused, and then he wanted to go down, as the hon. member for Marquette has done, into York-Sun-bury and flourish a telegram there and say: " One of the big implement people of Canada has refused to sell agricultural implements to the farmers and that is the reason why we are buying them in the United States." But such was not the answer he received. I have not made any canvass of the manufacturers, but I have stumbled across three who have not only offered to sell, but have sold, to the Grain Growers' organization. Does that prove that the manufacturers of Canada will not sell? When the Farmers' party made that statement, did they mean that every manufacturer had been tried by them and that every manufacturer had refused? If they did not, they had no business to use the words that they did. They might have said:
" Some manufacturers will not sell to us." They cannot say that all the manufacturers will not sell to them, because they have not tried them all. Some manufacturers who have wanted and who have tried to sell to them, have not been able to sell very

much, so that the Agrarian party have not very much grievance in that regard. The fact of the matter is that their whole opposition is against the implement industry in Canada, and when they can buy an article outside instead of inside the country, they are going to buy the article from an outside manufacturer. As was pointed out in this House on more than one occasion, the only Canadian-made article in a 100-page illustrated catalogue issued by them, was a wogon made in Petrolea. I think, perhaps, my hon. friend may recognize it. Whether they drove too hard a bargain, or whatever was the cause, the business that they gave that manufacturer was not long in shutting up the works, and it is a dead duck to-day. That was practically the only item manufactured in Canada amongst the implements advertised in the whole of their list. The United Farmers were offered the plant for a mere song. But did they buy it? No, they looked over it pretty carefully:	It was going at about
30 cents on the dollar, but there was so much money in making wagons that they did not think they would venture even that much in the business, so they did not buy it, and the business has since passed into the hands of another Brantford concern, by whom it is being run at the present time.
The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) tells us that free trade is a brilliant success with regard to binder twine, barbed wire, and cream separators. We have heard from the Prime Minister what happened to binder twine. If there is any one in the House who should know something about binder twine, I think I should, as I have lived almost within sight of two of the largest factories in Canada for a great many years. Binder twine was put on the free list some 12 or 15 years ago. At that time there were about 20 factories in Canada manufacturing binder twine. That number has since shrunk to three, and one of these is an American concern. The farmers did not even have pity on their own fellows, those who were in the same business as themselves, for the Farmers' Co-operative Binder Twine Company of Brantford was composed of about 4,000 farmers, just as good farmers as anybody, although they may not have been farming on as big a scale as some, but they had their money in this binder twine business, and at one time it was a great success, paying nearly 100 per cent in one year; but so drastic was the call of the West and so fierce were the denunciations of the Western farmers of a 10 per cent
duty on binder twine, which would have saved the business, that it was ruined, and the last remnants of that company are now being wound up. These 3,000 or 4,000 farmers who had their money in the concern, and owned it, were put out of business. The same thing happened with regard to a pork packing industry there, owned entirely by farmers. That was put out of business in a comparatively short time, but not by being put on the free list. However, they were handling a farm product that benefits right now, and always has for years, through the tariff. When my hon. friends of the Agrarian party tell us there is no benefit in the tariff to the farmer, I say that they do not know Ontario, although my hon. friend from Maple Creek (Mr. Maharg) ought to know Ontario, for he tells us he was born here. He must have forgotten more than he should have about his native province, when he can stand up - and say that the tariff does no good to the Canadian farmer.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am proud of it.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Proud of what you forgot?

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Proud of the province.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Then I do not see why you do not remember it a little in your policy. The policy you are pursuing is destructive to the farmer of Ontario. You ask the fruit growers of Ontario, of whom there are a large number, what they think of your policy, or the vegetable growers, or the man who produces poultry and eggs. My hon. friend from Marquette tells us that the farmer gets no benefit from the tariff. Why, only recently there were 600 tons of Chinese eggs imported into this country under a duty of 4 cents a dozen. I would not mind seeing the duty put at 10 cents a dozen if it would keep those eggs out.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We do not want that.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, because you do not raise chickens, but your chickens may come home to roost some day. I would like to have a little field day with my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Gould). If he will come up our way, we will take a bunch of farmers along to listen to us. He will draw the farmers, and I will try and give them the facts. I say that my hon. friends of the Agrarian party, many of whom came from Ontario, if they will consult the Ontario farmers, will find that the tariff has saved the farmers of Ontario.
My hon. friends talk about rural depopulation. I say that does not exist in our part

of the country. Our farmers have all the men they want. My hon. friends tell us, on the one hand, that they cannot sell their products at a profit, that hides are out of sight, that eggs, butter, cheese, wheat and all the rest of it are on the tumble, and then, on the other hand, they say: We will be saved if you populate the country-put more farmers on the land to raise more stuff that cannot be sold. That is a fine piece of argument, a beautiful demonstration of wit. They are going to be saved by getting more people to produce more of the stuff that they cannot sell now at a profit. I cannot imagine any other business in the world that would take that view. If my hon. friend wants to lose money, I would advise him to go into the plough business.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would cordially invite
my hon. friend to come to Assiniboia, as he has invited me out.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not know but
what I would feel more at home in my native province, from which my hon. friend also comes. I have not forgot the hole of the pit from whence I was digged. I have spoken in the West. I am not afraid to meet men who do not agree with me; I have met them before, and it may be that I shall meet them again in this House. I am not afraid to give the reason for the faith that is in me, and I say in all sincerity that the protective policy which has been followed in Canada for the past forty years has been to the vast advantage of the farmers of Ontario. That can be proved to a demonstration in every town and city of our province, and on every farm that is adjacent to those towns and cities, in which the farmers sell their produce and get their price. The home market is the best; it is the market that pays for the goods, and takes them off your hands immediately. My hon. friends seem to look upon the home market practically as a liability, instead of as an asset. They say, why cannot the implement manufacturer sell in Canada as cheaply as the United States manufacturer would sell without the duty? Let me tell them a few things that the manufacturer has to meet. In the first place, he has to settle with the Dominion Government on his profits-and that takes a large part of them. Then he has to take out a Dominion charter. Even that is not sufficient; he has to pay for a license in every province in which he does business. I know of one institution, Mr. Speaker, that before it could begin business had to pay out $200,000 in taxes, federal, provincial and municipal. My hon.

friends of the Agrarian party propose to let the American manufacturer who is over the border, and who has not paid one cent of these taxes-who has not supported a single one of, our municipal institutions, who has not given a dollar to schools, a dollar to churches, a dollar to charity, or a dollar to the province or municipality-* come into this country and divide the market with the man who has paid all these things. And they call that a square deal.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
How does the manu-,
facturer pay these taxes? Does he not pass them on to the consumer?

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He pays them in
cash.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Where does he get the
cash?

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As best he can.
Sometimes he borrows it.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He adds the taxes to the
price of the goods he sells.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend
knows that cash comes in slowly at times, especially if you have it loaned out, or have sold goods that are not paid for. My hon. friend who has lived so long in the West knows that there is quite an interval between the time that goods are soldi and the time they are paid for. This game of setting the farmer against the city man, and the city man against the farmer, is one that should not be indulged in. It cannot possibly lead to any good.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Who began it, and who has carried it on in this House during all this debate? I would not have made any of these remarks if hon. gentlemen across the way had not courted them by making a vicious attack upon manufacturers as a body, and in doing so, they attacked every working man and everybody that is employed in our towns and cities and is dependent. upon these industries for his living. The question was asked the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) a few moments ago, whether he stood by the Farmers' platform and believed in the 50 per cent reduction as a preference to British goods. He replied that he certainly did. He has also endorsed the Council of Agriculture's platform, which declares that they want free trade with Britain within five years. I think my hon. friend recognizes that as a correct statement. Well, what does free trade with Britain mean? Free trade with Britain simply

means free trade with, the world. I have pointed that out on many occasions to my hon. friends, but they cannot see it. Free trade with Britain would simply mean that goods from the United States would go to Liverpool and thence into Canada free; it would mean that German goods would go to Britain and then come free into Canada. And the same would be the case with French and Belgian goods and the products of other countries. My hon. friend shakes his head, but he knows that he could not stop these goods from coming into Canada free if we had free trade with Britain. My hon. friend knows that if three wells are connected by pipes the water will run freely from the first into the third though it has to go through the second; the water of all three will find the same level. So that my hon. friends, when they talk about free trade with Britain, are simply advocating free trade with the world, and if they have not got that fact into their heads they had better do so before they attempt to put this theory of theirs into practice. Let me repeat once more, for the benefit of those hon. gentlemen, that free trade with Britain is free trade with the world.
Those hon. gentlemen have denounced this Government for reckless expenditure and tremendous extravagance, and my hon. friend from Marquette, again, is the one who has principally made these charges. Let me ask the hon. gentleman this question: What about his own farmer government in Ontario? What about their spending proclivities? Has he a word to say in condemnation of them? Well, Sir, if the sample of government we have got from the Farmers in Ontario is to be taken as a fair example of what they would do for the whole of Canada, then, I say, the Lord help the country. The hon. Peter Smith, the great financier, of Ontario, in one year, the first year of his record, floated upwards of $70,000,000 worth of bonds in the name of the province. Think of it, Mr. Speaker. Seventy million dollars' worth of bonds in one year, a sum that ran the whole Dominion of Canada and more than ran it, when I first came into this House not so many years ago. And yet my Farmer friend has the temerity to talk about reckless extravagance! I hope he will send a wire to the Hon. Peter Smith, the Provincial Treasurer of Ontario, calling the attention of that gentleman to his denunciation in this House of reckless expenditures and unwarranted extravagance. Talk about road expenditures! Ask my friend from Hamilton and my friend from Wentworth; they can tell you something about road expenditures, and they have not got any kind of roads yet. Talk about reckless expenditure! Well, there is a guess coming to my hon. friend if he thinks that this country will save much by putting in an aggregation like that which we have in Toronto, which is the most reckless that the province has ever had, by all odds. There is no doubt about that fact, and if the hon. gentleman does .not believe it he can come up and look at the Government there. I tell you, Sir, we were caught napping. The expenditure there is the most reckless that the province has ever seen. They imposed new taxation, selecting five different ways. Four of them applied entirely to the cities and the fifth applied partly to the cities and partly to the country. That is the class of taxation they put on. So that if this is an example of what our good friends will give us when they get into power, I think we have gone far enough in the direction of putting our Farmer friends into governments in Canada.
My non. friend from Marquette says that the cream separator business has been a great success in Canada. Now, what cream separator does my hon. friend buy for his organization? If my information is correct he buys American cream separators, notwithstanding that he tells us the Canadian business was a great success under free trade. I am told-I may be wrong, but that is my information-that his organization is buying separators made in Buffalo. Those hon. gentlemen tell us that barbed wire, which was put on the free list, has also shown its ability to live. Well, I do not know where there is a barbed wire factory operating in Canada to-day. During the war, and practically at the very outset of the war, tens of thousands of tons of barbed wire were wanted for wire entanglements at the front, but we had not a factory in Canada, although, before this article was put upon the free list, there were twenty or thirty factories in this country devoting their attention largely to the barbed wire industry. But the whole industry was wiped out by the placing of this article on the free list, and that is what will happen to other industries if you put their manufactures on the free list. If these industries are ruined in this way the workingmen, who earn their bread by the sweat of their brow in the factories of the Dominion, will have to find homes elsewhere. Surely, in view of this, it will be admitted that the policy

which is proposed in this Budget, of moderate protection, is one of the best that can operate in Canada.
Now, I had not intended taking up so much time, but it was my wish to put on Hansard a few facts, with regard to the implement business, as prepared by the Massey-Harris Company and signed by Mr. Thomas Findlay, its president. He gives some interesting facts in a pronouncement submitted to the Finance Department. He outlines the history of the business from the year 1883 and shows that people can buy implements as cheaply in Canada as practically in any other country in the world; and the statement which is freely and often made that implements can be bought in all foreign countries cheaper than at home he proves to be entirely fallacious. He gives here the proof in regard to that and also deals with the statements made by my hon. friend from Victoria and Carle ton (Mr. Caldwell) with reference to what could be bought in Maine and in New Brunswick. He puts that hon. gentleman straight in a letter that was addressed to the department, showing that if the prices submitted by the hon. member had been taken advantage of and he had bought his implements in Maine instead of in New Brunswick he would have been money out of pocket. The hon. member is in the House and he probably remembers the figures he gave. The refutation is here in a letter which was sent to the Finance Department showing that my hon. friend, probably with no intentional unfairness, quoted the cash price in one instance and the credit price in the other. Well, Mr. Speaker, it is easy to show a difference if you do that. It costs something to give six months or a year's credit; and there is the interest.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman allow me to make a correction?

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I will not object to a Short statement, but I do not want a speech.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have the Massey-Harris price list-

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not want a price list. If I misrepresent my hon. friend he can correct me.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have the Massey-Harris price list, and-

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -the hon. member is not representing me fairly.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: This document has been carefully prepared. The firm went to the trouble of sending a special delegate to Maine to verify all the prices, to compare them with the prices in New Brunswick. When my hon. friend is on the platform down there he ought to be careful, because there may be some one watching him, and while he may get away with things on a platform, where there is no one to refute any wrong statement, nevertheless the facts can afterwards be obtained. And the fact is that, in this instance, he gave the cash price on the one hand and the credit price on the other.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is absolutely
false; I gave the cash prices in both cases.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am telling the
hon. gentleman what is in the letter that was carefully prepared, submitting all the facts. Now, Mr. Speaker, I think I have said enough to show that the policy that has been pursued in Canada with success for so many years in the development of our industries and in the building up of the country-not only the building up of our cities but the development of our natural resources-is one that is eminently in the interests of this country, and there is no doubt that Canada, in that policy is going in the right direction. In the matter of developing not only what may be called the city industries, but our natural resources-such as pulp, paper, minerals; all those things that go to build up a great industrial nation-Canada has embarked upon the right policy. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that if this policy is continued and pursued we will finally emerge from the difficulties and dangers in which the war has left us. Although matters do not look well at the present moment, although there are difficulties and dangers ahead, I believe they will be surmounted by united effort and by an honest determination on the part of our citizens to live and to let live. To raise any cry in the country to the jeopardy of a particular class is a dangerous policy. You may succeed in pulling down, but you will not succeed in building up by any such policy. Therefore I beseech hon. gentlemen on both sides that we should devote ourselves unitedly to the building up of all the industries of Canada, both urban and rural, and that as one united people we go on with a determined, honest effort to make the best of the grand heritage with which Providence has blessed us.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I entirely agree with
the sentiments expressed in his closing remarks by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat. We ought all to be united, and we ought all to follow the purpose that will tend to the building up of Canada. The question is, what is the best course to pursue'to attain that end? We have listened to the speech of the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt). He is still a high protectionist, and he has expressed again this afternoon the views which he has uttered in this House and in the country session after session, and year after year. I have no doubt the hon. gentleman is absolutely sincere in his views but we on this side cannot see eye to eye with him, and it is for the people of Canada to decide which is the best policy to adopt. The Budget brought down by the Finance Minister may be satisfactory to hon. gentlemen opposite, but there is one thought that occurs to me, as it would accur to the ordinary individual: I cannot quite grasp the legerdemain of the book-keeping which declares that, although the expenditures exceed the revenues by $101,000,000, and that amount has been added to the national debt, therefore we still have a surplus. To the ordinary man such a proposition as that is a conundrum, and I do not believe the country will take very much stock in it.
Now as to the Budget, and the tariff proposals which accompany it, are concerned, I would point out first this fact: for a long time past this Government has maintained that there would be tariff revision; to that end a commission, headed by the Minister of Finance, has travelled from one end of Canada to the other, and I read the statement in one newspaper that evidence had been taken to the extent of two million words. We were told that the tariff would be revised and placed in such a condition as to satisfy the whole of the people of Canada. Following the tariff inquiry Parliament is called, the representatives of the people assemble, the Budget is delivered-and there is no general revision of the tariff such as we were led to believe would take place. What reason is given for this? That on account of some contemplated changes in the tariff of the United States it would not be well to make any change in our own tariff at the present time. Let us see how well that excuse pans out. There was an election in East Elgin on November 22, 1920. The Prime Minister visited that constituency and he said "Elect our candidate and we
promise you that when the next session of Parliament comes there will be a revision of the tariff. We are now collecting the necessary information to that end. The Tariff Commission is now going from one end of the country to the other making an inquiry, and we will give you a tariff revision." Parliament met on February 14, last and in the speech from the Throne tariff revision was promised. However it has not taken place. Surely it cannot be argued that delay is due to the Fordney Bill, or the Young Bill. Because, at the very time the Prime Minister spoke, on the occasion alluded to, the terms of the Fordney Bill were known. Then what excuse or logical reason is there for the Government's failure to implement its promise and revise the tariff? The reason, to my mind, is to be found in this fact: The high protectionist friends of the Government descended in a flock upon them and said "Leave the tariff alone if you have the slightest regard for your life." The tariff has been practically left alone. In so far as regards any changes that have gone into effect, these changes mean more taxation and a further raising of the cost of the people's food. What do we find in the Government's Budget proposals? Taxation of the necessities of life; the duties on cocoa, chocolate, and so forth increased; increased taxation applied to arrowroot biscuits, an article that plays an important part in the diet of infants; and a further upward lift to sugars. The Minister of Finance may be proud of such tariff changes as these, but of the articles to which I have alluded there is not one that is not an actual necessity of life, or that does not form part of the ordinary everyday meal of the masses of people. On a former occasion I suggested to the Finance Minister the proper course for him to pursue. I shall not now repeat the views which I then expressed except to say this-If the Government desires to impose taxation let it place that taxation on luxuries, and reduce the imposts on the necessities of life to the greatest extent possible. We have in this country the most serious unrest that Canada has ever witnessed. Will that unrest be allayed by the imposition of further burdens upon the people? No; the right policy to pursue is to make that taxation as low as possible and to leave free of taxation as far as possible the necessities of life. Not very long ago a friend of mine, Mr. McKinnon -who I believe is President of the Manufacturers' Association-found fault with

certain of my remarks on the subject of high protection and in reference to my having said that he was "a Haman's gallows man" Mr. McKinnon declared that he did not think I knew what the expression meant. Well, I have not read the book of Esther of late, but my recollection of the Haman incident is this: that Haman was a man who erected a high gallows for the purpose of hanging a certain people and had all his arrangements completed, when suddenly it was found that Haman was not all that he appeared to be, and he was hanged on the very gallows that he had prepared for others. Now, may it not be that the Government, in still pursuing their tariff policy of higher taxation on the necessaries of life, will find themselves in a political sense, in the same plight as Haman, at the impending general- election?
I am not going into an analogy on tariffs, but while listening the other day to my hon. friend from Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) I could not help thinking that of late there seems to have come, over this House a tendency to depreciate Great Britain. We are told:	Oh, no, you
must not copy the fiscal policy of England, because she is becoming decadent. Let me say, Mr. Speaker, that any country that could have done what Great Britain did during the war-in the field, in financing so many of her Allies, in transporting a large proportion of the United States soldiers across the Atlantic, and in furnishing munitions and equipment, and that today is able to reduce her national debt by $200,000,000, is not very decadent. To say the least, we need not be ashamed of her being at the head of our Confederation, so to speak. To my mind she has shown that she is absolutely the leading country in the world. Apparently the fiscal arrangements of Great Britain are satisfactory to her people, and I for one do not think that it comes with any very good grace from hon. members to decry Great Britain and, in effect, to say to her people: You do not know what you are doing with your economic system; you ought to do thus and so because we in Canada think you should. It appears to me that in our present position we have ample to occupy our time in looking after our own business without bothering the people of our great Mother Country, and I think that if we stick to a purely Canadian platform we will he fulfilling the duty for which we were sent here by our constituents.
The trouble with Canada, so far as I can make out, is that she needs to extend

her foreign trade. If we would build up our manufacturing and farming interests we must find them more markets for the sale of their products. In this connection I would direct attention to the flourish of trumpets with which my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne) brought down his statement of operations of his mercantile marine. But it seems to me that it would have been well had the Minister of Finance taken the Minister of Marine and Fisheries gently aside and said to him: You have already spent millions and are to-day proposing to spend more millions on your mercantile marine; hut in our present financial condition with our per capita debt almost $300, this is not the time to spend more money on a doubtful venture, and you had better cut your vote in two. Had that been done the money so saved could have been devoted to extending our foreign trade and letting the world know that Canada was on the map and ready with the goods and willing to trade. It has been predicted, and I am sorry to say that I believe the prediction will come true, that between now and another year we will have this mercantile marine, this creation of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, a white elephant on the hands of the people, and he will have to sell the ships for a quarter of what he paid for them. What is the good of repeating the argument? In all the ports of the world you have bottom after bottom absolutely idle. I saw a statement the other day that although these ships of our mercantile marine cost between one and two hundred dollars a ton, there are ships lying in the Clyde to-day which would answer our purposes and which could be bought for $25 a ton. That statement was made by one of the very best informed shipping men in the Dominion after a recent trip to England; I refer to Mr. James Playfair, whom, no doubt, the minister knows. If freights are going to be hard to get, and unremunerative when you do get them, would not our money have been far better spent in the way I have suggested than in building more ships to rust at their berths? It appears to me that had proper allowance been made for depreciation, and so forth, the Minister of Marine would have had no surplus to show on the past year's operations of his mercantile marine; and it is pretty certain that even his present method of book-keeping will not enable him to disguise the deficit next

year, which will likely run into many more millions of dollars.
Taking into consideration the deficit on our mercantile marine and also the huge deficit on our railway operations, where are the people of Canada to get off at? How are we going to meet these enormous liabilities? This year our railway deficit is $69,000,000, and next year it is prophesied that it will be increased to $168,000,000. If this Government keeps on with its extravagant waste of the moneys of our people, numbering scarcely 9,000,000, what position shall we be landed in? Have the Government curtailed their extravagance? They have not. As the hon. member for Marquette said to-day, the extravagance still goes on, the money flows like water, and no heed is taken of the present or the future.
In so far as our railways are concerned we have adopted the principle of public ownership. I do not say that the Government did not have to take the railways over, but now that they have got those railways, I say frankly that I have yet to be convinced that government ownership is the proper thing. But if it is to be made a success two factors are essential; in the first place, there must be complete elimination of even a colourable resemblance of the interests that were formally associated with the railways which have now become part of our national system. I have great respect for Mr. D. B. Hanna, and in making these remarks I do not desire to reflect upon him; I think he is a perfectly honourable and a perfectly just man. But, Sir, Mr. Hanna is unfortunate. There is no question about the fact that among the people of the country generally -among	Liberals, Conservatives and
farmers alike-there is an absolute distrust of Mackenzie and Mann. The people feel that the country was bled, not for the purposes of the Canadian Northern but for the benefit of subsidiary enterprises, thus bringing gain to the pockets of these two men. If therefore, the confidence of the people is to be regained, everything coloured with Mackenzie and Mann must be absolutely taken out of the management of the Government railways. There are rumours abroad to-day-whether or not they are true I do not know-that Sir William Mackenzie is still exceedingly active and exceedingly close to the management of the national railways so far as the Canadian Northern portion of it is concerned. Is it possible that Sir William, with his boundless ambition and with
his control of millions on the part of himself and his friends, is to-day angling for the ownership of the Canadian National railways? If anythink like that should happen, I have only to say that it would be a great calamity for the people. Therefore I submit that the first thing to do is to remove all traces of Mackenzie and Mann from the present management of the Canadian National railways.
The next step I deem to be necessary is this: There are many advocates of public ownership in Canada. The principle may be right, and it may be wrong; I have yet to be convinced. But if you are to have public ownership of any enterprise you must have at the head of the management, or included in the board of management, persons who believe in the principle of public ownership. The Government should, therefore at the earliest possible moment, in the reorganization of the management of these public roads, put at the head of that management or include in it men who have the utmost faith in public ownership and are in sympathy with it. If you do not do so, if you have on the board of management men who are entirely out of sympathy -with the principle of public ownership, these men are very human, and the best efforts may not be put forth.
Coming to the speech delivered by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) in this House the other day, I would say that the keynote of it-to be candid, the only note in the speech-was a manifestation of curiosity to know something about hon. gentlemen on this side of the House. The right hon. gentleman said that there was no Liberal party, and the hon. Minister. of Militia (Mr. Guthrie) has said: So far as the Liberal party isv concerned, we have them all; you have only a remnant. The right hon. gentleman in his speech the other day went from one subject to the other but he always came back to the same theme, "Oh tell me; for heaven's sake tell me, where are the Liberal party? Where are the Farmers' party? What are you going to do? Where do you stand? Please tell me so that I may know." It was like the man who had committed a murder and who had succeeded more or less in putting the thought of it from his mind; but just as he would be feeling that he had everything covered up and that everything was all right, the head of the poor murdered man would pop up and scare him to death. Time and again during the course of my right hon. friend's speech-in the middle, at the end, at the

three-quarter pole-he repeated: "Where are the Liberals? Where are the Farmers? What are they going to do?" Well, all I have' to say to the right hon. gentleman is this: The Liberals are here; they are quite content, happy, and waiting. The farmers are there, and none of them look to me like a "dilapidated annex." They all look strong; they all look healthy; they are there, content and also waiting. The Prime Minister says there is no Liberal party. He would give us to believe that he has nothing to fear; that the good old Tory party is still uppermost in Canada; that the old flag is still waving. Well, in order to gratify his overweening curiosity I would say to him that there is only one way to get an answer to all this questioning: appeal to the ppople and let them say. The people do not often go wrong. They are sane, the people of Canada; they know their way about pretty well. They have set ideas, and when they get an idea into their head they generally see that it is carried out. I strongly recommend to the Prime Minister, therefore, that he dissolve the House, go to the country, and say to the people: "I am not sure where these fellows opposite stand, and I want to know; the only way I can possibly know is through your verdict." Let the Government go ahead and try it. It is quite simple.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Because the Government would be beaten and this side would be returned to power.
There is nothing in the Budget, Mr. Speaker, having in view a reduction in the cost of living, but there is much in it which will tend to increase the taxation. I propose to vote for the amendment because I think it will help to remedy that state of affairs. Just here, Sir, may I be permitted to make a digression? In 1896 Sir Wilfrid Laurier formed a Cabinet. It was referred to as the "Cabinet of all the talents"; it was a galaxy, Sir, of clever men-of men who had the interests of this country at heart, men of foresight, men who had a proper conception of the needs of this country. In every way it came up to the expectations of the people as well as the expectations of the great Leader who formed it. In this House and in this present Canadian Parliament, we have but one of those men left.
I know I voice the sentiment of every man on this side of the House, and I am sure I voice the sentiment of every man on either side and especially the sentiment

of the people of the Dominion of Canada, when I say that we all hope and pray that long may he (Mr. Fielding) be spared with his wise counsel, with his keen insight into the needs of the people, to help to guide and shape the destinies of this great Dominion of ours.
Now in closing:	Though neither a
prophet, nor the son of a prophet, I make this prophecy. Whether an election comes soon or late, an election must come, and the opinion of the people of the Dominion of Canada must be had; and my firm belief is that when that time comes, we shall have, as Minister of Finance in a Liberal Government, the man who brought down the tariff of 1897 and who made this country prosperous and happy, and that under his wise guidance a tariff will be so framed as to meet the needs of all the people of the Dominion. I believe that that will come about, and that he will be the man under whom the economic policies of the Dominion of Canada will be carried out. Let me say this to the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton), that then not only the sun, but the moon and the stars, will shine; not only the rivers, but all the waters will sparkle; and the people of this country will be brought back to an era of prosperity that they have not known for some time.
At Six o'clock, the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at Eight o'clock.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in opening my remarks I desire in the first instance to commend the Fin- * ance Minister (Sir Henry Drayton) and the Government for the way in which they have handled the present serious situation in our country. I believe that the wisdom of their policy will become more and more evident to the people of Canada as time goes on.
We are confronted to-day with a number of very serious problems. We have a business depression, and almost unprecedented unemployment throughout the country. The outlook for the sale of our surplus farm products is very unpromising; the revenues of the country are on the decline; our obligations are very great, and I believe, may become greater; our railway rates are too high, and our Government railway lines are losing money. All these things were inevitable after the Great War, with its inflation, and the deflation which had to follow. Canada so far has

weathered the storm and in my opinion is giving every promise of establishing her business and finance on a sound basis. We in this country have every reason to be thankful that, considering all we had to go through, we are in such a good position I can recall no other country in the world that can be regarded as being in as good a position as Canada to-day.
The manufacturing industries of our country are under attack at the present time, and those who are engaged in them feel that it is necessary that they should justify their existence. In relation to all the problems which I have just mentioned, I would like to say that I believe that unless the manufacturing industries of this country are properly handled, all these problems will become intensified. In a crisis such as we are facing to-day, when a great issue is raised, it becomes imperative that we should face it frankly and leave no doubt as to where we stand with regard to it. A great issue has been raised; it is an old one, it is true, but what has happened in recent years has made it stand out more prominently than at any time in the past, and the action that we may take as a country to-day is going to be of greater importance to the interest and welfare to the people of Canada than any similar action we might have taken in the past.
It is my intention, Mr. Speaker, to try and make my position perfectly clear upon the issue of protection or free trade, because after all it seems to me that we can take only one of two positions. A man may in his belief in free trade as the proper policy for this country adopt an intermediate course, but by so doing he will definitely align himself as one who proposes to advance towards free trade at the earliest possible moment, and he also must take the ground that this country made a mistake when it ever departed from the policy of free trade. So far as I am concerned, after considerable experience of the tariff and its effects, and after having given some thought to the question, I have come to the conclusion that this country .took the only course that it was proper for it to take when it decided to adopt the principle of protection in its fiscal legislation. On that platform I am prepared to stand, as well as behind the policy outlined by the Prime Minister when he spoke to the House a few days ago.
In my opinion we should make some departure from the way in which we now deal with the tariff problems of this country. I believe that the people of this
country whose business it is to know about the tariff and its effects upon them should be put in a position where they may better understand the value of the tarjff and of protection, where they may understand the burdens that they may carry temporarily or permanently, in order that this policy may be carried out in the interests of the people of Canada as a whole. In order to do this, I feel that our machinery or organization is not fully equipped for handling tariff questions, and the relations of the tariff to the people of Canada and of other countries. If a conference were called-and such a thing might not be a bad idea-comprising representatives of labour, of the manufacturers, the merchants, the railroads and the producing industries such as mining, lumber, etc., together with representatives of the consuming public, they would not discuss the question as we deal with it on the floor of the House. I believe they would try to co-operate and find out what were really the facts, what was the best policy, and how it would affect the various interests involved. Such a conference, in my opinion, would not disperse before unanimously demanding that the Government should establish a tariff board, or a board of experts similar to that in the United States. The member for Victoria and Carleton (Mr. Caldwell) made the statement in the House that the Manufacturers' Association were asking for such a board with powers practically to usurp those of the Government. Such a request was never made by the Manufacturers' Association. I have their resolution here, although I do not propose to read it; but what they did ask for was that a board be appointed that would give information and advice and that would submit all the facts it might gather with regard to the tariff and its relations to the people. We must have a railway board to deal with railway rates, and that is not so complicated or important a matter as the tariff is to this country. Now the Manufacturers' Association, in asking for this board, gives us evidence that they do not desire to conceal the facts with regard to the subject. They desire the facts to be known, and they are prepared to justify their position. They have such faith in their position that they feel it would commend itself to the people of Canada as being one that could be sustained. Hundreds of labour organizations have also passed resolutions requesting that such a board be formed. I might
