speechtext:
say, for the information of the hon. member for Victoria and Carleton, that in the United States, where the question was first mooted, it was the farmers' organization which was most insistent that such a board should be established, and since it has been formed the work it has done for the country has been so valuable that there-has been no thought, on the part of any party, of going back to the old system.
During the months of the fall, representatives of the Government travelled through the country gathering information on the tariff, and I am told that, in bulk, the pages containing the evidence taken are about three feet thick. I believe it would be quite impossible to-day to use that evidence to any great extent because much of it would be out of date. Now, in making this suggestion, I do not reflect in any degree whatever upon the Government, because some time ago a former government, of which several hon. gentlemen at present occupying seats on the Treasury benches were members, endeavoured to bring about such a reform. All I can say is that if they introduce it I cannot see how it could have anything but the heartiest support of members of the House, and I believe it would do a very great deal towards removing the misunderstanding with regard to the effect of our laws upon the people. There is a great fear in minds of many people that at present a few persons sit down in a room and try to decide this question without sufficient facts and an adequate knowledge of the whole situation, and that they are influenced in their decisions by political or other interests. That may or may not be so; we do not know; we are all human. But the tariff is the business of the public, and I feel that the door should be open and that all the facts should be laid before the people. Then we should be sure that whatever action was taken would have the support of the people, and its permanency would contribute greatly to the prosperity of the country.
Now to come to the question of protection. The first thing we must fix in our minds is what is best for the welfare of the country. It is in the interest of no particular class and of no particular province; it is a question of protecting our own nation. Are we not going to use any legitimate weapon to defend ourselves in a world in which practically every other country-I would say every other country-exerts what powers it has

to defend and develop itself? Great Britain has her own way of protecting herself, and in her commercial dealings she adopts the same principle as any other country; that is to say, she does that which she considers best for herself. If I believed in free trade I would look upon this as a country that was to be made free for any one to come into it and use its resources in any way he saw fit so long as he did what was legal; and it would seem to me that the logical conclusion, from this statement, would be that there should be the same freedom with regard to immigration, and that we should permit the free entry of any person who desired to come to our shores. But we do not believe in that principle, and I do not see how it is possible for any one to contend that free trade is really a practical question in Canada to-day. If we believe in protection, therefore, the question is not whether it is high, or low, or moderate; it is a principle we apply as a physician would give treatment to a patient. It may be that at times high protection, like strong medicine, is the best thing to administer; but no one contends that it should be habitual. I think that .it is best in this country, generally speaking, that we should have a medium or moderate protection; but the defenders of high protection can cite many instances of the success of that policy, particularly in the United States, where it has achieved such splendid results in building up that great country.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have tried to follow the debate rather closely, and to pick out some of the points that I felt I was in a position to give special attention to, and in bringing these forward I do not wish it to appear in any way that I think any hon. member is endeavouring to mislead the House. What I do know is, that there is a very great misunderstanding with regard to this whole question; and I do feel that the Government took the right and proper stand when it decided that it was not in the interest of this country that an election should be brought on during the abnormal times that have existed up to the present. I would use as an illustration this fact- that up to a very short time ago, the business interests of this country were in the position where it could be said that they had reaped very large profits. During the time of inflation large paper profits, or book profits, were made; but during the past few months a large part of these profits, and in some instances all the accu-

mulation of the years of the war, have been swept away. Not only that, but many of these companies have paid heavy taxation to the Government and to-day owe the Government amounts of money on which they are paying interest, and they are unable, with their working capital, to continue the operation of their plants. It would not have been fair to the people of this country to have brought on an election at such a time as that; it would be like trying a prisoner without giving him an opportunity to properly place the evidence before an unprejudiced jury. What have we now? We see the other side, and it was only due to the people that this Government should have held off an election until they could see the other side of the question. Not only is the situation as I have stated but for some years, upon a thousand platforms in this country, the position of the great industries of Canada have been grossly misrepresented. By so stating, I do not mean that the misrepresentation has been intentional; it has been through ignorance and a lack of knowledge of the situation. The other evening the member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Thomson) made this astounding statement :
I say that under the present tariff we shall be paying to the manufacturers of Canada a bonus equal to $500,000,000 a year.
Mr. Speaker, I have tried to find out what the manufacturers' total profits are in Canada in a normal year. I have tried to arrive at it from different angles. The Census Bureau purposely covers that up because they have not the right to bring out those facts; but at least we can find out very easily by inquiry there that the manufacturers cannot make $500,000,000 a year. However, there was another way I tried to ascertain the facts, and that was from the taxation which is paid. We have a business profits tax and that tax has yielded about $40,000,000 a year. But all of that taxation is not on the manufacturing industries-all the great jobbing houses, and all the great retail stores-some of them like the T. Eaton Company and many other large institutions scattered through the length and breadth of the country-also pay that tax. In order to be very generous in the figures that I am using I therefore place the amount that the manufacturers might have paid at $34,000,000. In addition, we have the income tax on those corporations that would come under the business profits tax, that totals $13,400,000' but I would reduce that down to $8,000,000, and it yields a grand total of $42,000,000. Now when you consider that the minimum tax was 10 per cent, and a great many returns it was 25, 50 and 75 per cent, you will see how absurd is the statement, from that standpoint, that the manufactures can be presented with $500,000,000 yearly. My estimate is that the profits on three billion dollars of manufactures would run about $180,000,000, taking such favourable times as we have during the past couple of years, or an average of about 6 per cent net profit on the turn over.
It is not very much.

Perhaps not, but there is many a manufacturer who would be very thankful if he were assured that amount, and during this year there will be very few that will enjoy any such profit.
The member for Qu'Appelle in his figures overlooked several very important facts. *First, he overlooked the duty on the equipment; next, the duty on the materials, or parts, that enter into the finished article; third, the tax on the companies' profits; fourth, the tax on the dividends. In his computation he also overlooked the fact that the price is not fixed by the United States price plus the duty. In last year's customs returns I find that the importation of machines for manufacturers amounted to over $33,000,000 on which a duty of $8,336,000 was paid; and in looking through the many items in the report of the Customs Department it will be found that probably the largest amount of duties are drawn direct from the manufacturers for their partly finished goods or raw materials. For example on the item of steel the duties paid amounted to $5,623,650; including on angles and parts $1,216,000; on rolled iron for making milling cutters $706,000; also tubing for boilers and beds $578,000; wire $430,000; and fuel $4,865,000. It will therefore be seen how absurd it is for a man to charge a manufacturer with having put in his pocket all the amount of the duty that the schedule calls for on his goods. As a matter of fact he has not that protection. In a great many instances he has not one-half of it, because you must make due allowance for the duty he has bo pay on his imported material. Now not only is that a fact, but the manufacturer also reduces the price to a point where internal competition compels him to go; and in all the experience that I have had in any businesses that I am connected with-and I

am interested in several companies and know the existing conditions-I do not know of any case in twenty years where the price of the article sold in Canada was regulated by the price in the United States plus the duty. Protection does not make a contribution to a manufacturer any more than it makes a contribution to the employees who work for that industry. It simply makes it possible for the employees to secure work at fair wages, and for the capitalist to employ his capital at a reasonable rate, or otherwise competition will soon bring it down to the point where it is reasonable. There may be isolated instances of abuse, and it is to reach them that we should have a board of inquiry functioning. It has been my opinion that if this House had appointed a board to deal with the tariff and see that it was not abused, instead of appointing the Board of Commerce, we would have made much better progress.
Another thing overlooked was the tax upon profits. In fact, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Thomson) evidently forgot that whilst the business profits tax has been repealed the income tax on corporation profits has not, and that if a company makes, a profit of only one per cent on its capital it has to pay ten per cent of that to the Government, less an exemption of $2,000. If the company makes a profit of 10 per cent or 20 per cent the rate is the same. This I think should be amended and a graduated scale should be adopted. There are many companies to-day that will feel that tax very severely, but no complaints have been heard from them.
We will suppose that one man owns a company on the operations of which he makes $50,000 profit. His exemption of $2,000 leaves $48,000 subject to the ten per cent tax, which, plus five per cent supertax, represents a total taxation of $5,040. If he takes that profit out of his business he is taxed again to the extent of $5,050 by the supertax, or $10,090 altogether. And in speaking of the profits we must always remember that it is not the gross profits, it is the actual amount that in the end is left with the owner of the business. The manufacturer is also used as the medium for the collection of this sales tax to a very large extent. He has to pay one and a half per cent on his materials, and if he has sold his goods ahead he has to take another half a cent off his margin in that respect. He has also to collect the sales tax of one and a half per cent on goods sold to jobbers and

of three per cent if sold to retailers. When we look over the list of taxes collected from our industries, does it not appear that one should not be too hasty in getting up in this House and saying: We. have adopted a platform of free trade in the implements of production? I think it is a mistake for any political party to put itself on record to do anything whatever to this tariff until that party has had an opportunity of investigating its operation and giving the people concerned an opportunity of defending themselves. That is one serious objection I have to the platform of the official Opposition.
Another statement made by the hon. [DOT] member for Mackenzie was as follows:
I find that our customs tariff taxation per capita last year was $22.55, whereas the United States tariff taxation per capita was $3.15.
Then he works it out and continues:
It should also be remembered that to that taxation we are adding a sales tax which will represent a total payment in the case of the average Canadian family of $147.75.
That seems to me a most illogical position to take, because they have claimed no matter whether they can prove it or not, that the rate of duty on goods made in Canada is the amount taken out of the consumer in Canada, even though a manufacturer may sell his goods here as cheap as on the other side; but in the statement referred to they take the amount paid at the frontier as the basis for taxation. It is the high tariff in the United States that keeps out imports and therefore the comparative figures are not such as to permit us to arrive at any conclusion. Then the "average family" illustration is not a fair way of arriving at the expenses of an ordinary family. Why, all one has to do is to read over the list of taxes that were collected through the customs to find that the average family is interested in very little of the articles mentioned in the returns. Our legislation has been directed towards taking the burden off the average family. Take only three items-automobiles, engines, and boilers, and machines, on which customs tax was paid to the extent of $22,500,000. How ridiculous it is to assert that a workingman's family is paying $147 a year in tariff taxation. Any one could take the articles they buy and easily prove that the tariff tax paid is a very small amount indeed.
My good friend from Mackenzie also made this further statement:
We, on the other hand, claim that while the Government receives $1 from the customs revenue tax, our good friends, the manufacturers,

receive $3. If this is not correct, I am sure my good friends sitting opposite will show me that it is not so.
The arguments I have already advanced should make it clear to every hon. member-that that could not possibly be so. He -would say that we are presenting the manufacturers with $495,000,000; but it is questionable if after their taxation is taken off they have a third of that in profits. These are very unfortunate statements, and I would ask my good friends to investigate a little more closely before they make such comments. What we want is not to throw dust in the eyes of the people; we want to try and take it out. And it does not seem to me that Parliament is the place where statements Should be made that have not been very carefully weighed.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we have been told that in 1898 certain articles were put on the free list, and that the various industries concerned had been able to succeed notwithstanding the loss of protection. I have had a special opportunity of being in touch with some of those industries and I am going to deal with the binder twine situation. In 1898 we imported 2,405,000 pounds; in 1917, 66,000,000 pounds, or more than twenty-five times as much; but that is not an average year. However, I have a statement before me compiled a year ago from the latest returns I could get from the customs and the statistical branch, which shows that the amount of twine made in Canada for the years 1917 and 1918 was
59.000.	000 pounds; we imported 115,000,-
000 pounds and deduct exported 19,000,000 pounds; and the total we used was 155,000,000 pounds.	[DOT]
Deducting from the amount of binder twine made in Canada during those years
59.000.	000 pounds, the amount of exports,
19.000.	000 pounds, we find that the amount of Canadian-made binder twine used in Canada was 40,000,000 pounds, or only 26 per cent of tne total. Now, the member for Qu'Appe'ie suggested that industries should be encouraged that could work on a 10 per cent protection. Well, all that is asked by the company referred to to-day, the Brantford Cordage Company, is 5 per cent, and they say that the benefits that would accrue to the country would be very great. The extra freight resulting in shipments to the West would amount to over $700,000, and that would go to the benefit of our railways. The importation of the raw material ly the west coast from the Philippine Islands would yield freights
amounting to $212,500, or a total of $912,500. I give tnese figures also in order to show the extent to which the protection of the industries of this country has a bearing upon the railway situation. I would place myself on record as saying that we would be wise in affording a small protection to binder twine and believe that if a board or commission would make careful inquiry i' to the matter and examine the subject in all its bearings, they would recommend that that be done. Here is an item which I clipped out of a western paper last year; it is from Kelwood:
There is a continued scarcity along the line of gasoline. Binder twine supplies seem hazardous at the present time and old stocks have been depleted by farmers buying in advance. There is a serious shortage of barbed wire.
Then it say-.:
The district convention of the Grain Growers' Association will be held at Kelwood on July 10.
I hope that on that occasion this question was taken into serious consideration and that the grain growers there assembled considered whether it is advantageous that Canada's supply of binder twine should come almost entirely from the United States. They take their crop off first and if the necessary provision is not always made to supply Canada we are likely to go seriously short some day. The farmers' organization should take this matter up and try to help the binder twine interests to get reasonable protection, because thereby the interests of the farmers themselves will be protected.
With regard to barbed wire, in 1897, before the duty was taken off, we imported that commodity to the value of $80,467 while in 1920 we imported $2,056,000 worth. In 1918 we manufactured barbed wire only to he value of $300,000 for war purposes. Th? t does not look as if the industry had been a success under free trade. With regard to cream separators, I should like to point out that the situation in this regard was a somewhat peculiar one, due to the fact than many of these cream separators were patented articles and thus had a market in Canada assured to them by agreements with the patentees. Many of the most prominent makes of cream separators have an exclusive sale in Canada, and there is no competition from the same machine on the part of any other country.
In conclusion, I should like to give some reasons why we desire that our industries shall be continued in a vigorous and

healthy state. We believe that the industries are essential to our welfare because of the diversified employment they give to our people, the large home market they create for our products and natural resources, and' the extent to which they contribute to the strength and development of our railways. Our railways are the arteries, the veins and the capillaries which carry the life blood of commerce back and forth to every part of our Dominion-to the farm, the forest and the mine; and the industries keep alive and add increasing power to our banks and financial institutions. They also indirectly help the professional men and the merchants and affect directly or indirectly practically all other interests and activities of the country. The Government stands by this policy not with any desire to further special interests of the manufacturers, but with the laudable object of attaining the largest measure of unity, prosperity and national upbuilding.

Mr. Speaker, I wish in the first place to congratulate the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Harold) upon his very great effort as a former Liberal to justify his position in remaining as a supporter of the present Administration. I wish also to direct attention to the fact that of the seven important speeches delivered by members supporting the Government five were delivered by former Liberals and supporters of the great Liberal party from 1896 to 1911, when it administered the country's affairs so satisfactorily that in 1911, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Poster) could only say throughout the length and breadth of Canada:	" Let well
enough alone." It looks as if the present Administration is trying to commercialize these five hon. gentlemen, trying to send out word to the different parts of the country that on the Government benches there are five outstanding figures, gentlemen who assisted in carrying on the affairs of Canada when every person was so weli pleased with the conduct of the Government that they cried:	Let well enough
alone; take no chances of doing anything to bring about better times and to increase prosperity throughout the country.
Mr. Speaker, contrast the message to which I have just referred with that handed out by the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) the other day. Did he say: Let well enough alone? No, that was not his cry. These are his words:
	.
Mr. Speaker, we in Canada have a great task before us. The world is sadly out of tune. May we help in restoring harmony? Trust and confidence are sadly lacking. Class interests are advanced with selfish insistence. Unemployment is with us. Faith in our fellow-men is weakened. Doubt of the future is often voiced. And what is the trouble?
What is the trouble, Mr. Speaker? I will endeavour to give you a few reasons for the trouble, after I read the following sentence which was quoted in part by the member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) this afternoon. The Minister of Finance said:
The sun still shines-the rivers still sparkle 

our lands are as great and fruitful as ever.
For these three great blessings mentioned by the minister we have to thank Providence, not the Government or the Minister of Finance.	.
"What is the trouble?" the Minister of Finance asks. All he has to do is to do as hon. gentlemen on this side have already called upon him to do. The people of Canada are so dissatisfied with the present Administration in their conduct of affairs of this country that they are bound to tell him what the trouble is, and, as the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Pardee) said this afternoon, let the Government appeal to the country and they will find out what the trouble is; they will have an answer, and without question they will have it in abundance.
As regards the present Budget, this is what you will find the people in the different cities and towns and in the country districts saying when they are asked if there is anything wrong with the tax which the Government has placed in this Budget of $10 a case on spirits. They say that while the referendum was held in Ontario on April 18, the day that importation into the province was prohibited was May 1, so that some days elapsed allowing the richer people, the men with plenty of money to fill their cellars and attics with all the spirits they might require for future years. Thus, the Government gave the man of wealth an advantage over the man in humble circumstances who might want a case or a bottle of liquor for different reasons. The man in humble circumstances is the man who is now called upon to pay the tax on liquor which he requires for medicinal and other purposes. Yet the Minister of Finance asks: "What is the trouble?"
Hon. gentlemen may laugh, but the people of the country do not consider this Budget any laughing matter. The necessaries of

life are being taxed by the present Budget. The Minister of Finance, in his address, stated that oatmeal and flour in packages under 48 pounds would be taxed. The man who has the means can purchase flour in 50 or 100-pound sacks or in barrels, and thus escape paying the tax; but the mechanic, who receives a weekly wage, hands his wages over to his wife on Saturday, and when she goes to the store to buy food, clothing and shoes, and to pay for her rent, light and heat, she is the one who has to pay the tax. She does not buy flour by the hundredweight, but she buys flour 12 or 25 pounds at a time. Is it not ridiculous on the part of the present Administration to say to that woman: "You will have to pay a tax on your flour if you buy it in less than 50 pound packages." Yet the minister asks: "What is the trouble?" The trouble is that the Government is not giving a square deal to the ordinary people of this country, but is giving an advantage to the wealthy classes.
Hon. gentlemen on this side of the House have drawn the attention of the Government to the fact that men on the mail and customs staffs, who are receiving small salaries ranging from only $900 to $1,000, are getting a cut of 25 per cent in their bonus, and yet the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) stands up in this House and defends the action of the Administration in that regard. Let me draw the attention of hon. members to the Esti-
9 p.m. mates which we have been passing from time to time. In every department you will find officials, who are drawing salaries ranging from $2,000 to $4,000 a year, receiving a handsome raise of from $100 to $300, and the man with the humble salary is receiving a 25 per cent cut in his bonus. Nevertheless, the Minister of Finance asks: What is the trouble? Let him go to towns and villages where the rural mail is delivered by men under contract at about $850 a year, out of which they have to keep a couple of horses. If these men have not a legal right, they have a moral right to be given an opportunity by this Government to get a living wage with which they may be able to look after their boys and girls and give them an education as any other parent would. But the Government hangs on to that paltry little contract and makes these men go through the storms of winter and heat of summer on a salary of $850 a year. If this Government was worthy of handling the affairs of this great country, the first thing it would do would be to say: "We will give to these
men a bonus so that they may raise their families respectably and, perhaps, some of their sons may be outstanding men in the future in this great Dominion of Canada. Yet the Minister of Finance asks: "What is the trouble?"
This afternoon we heard from the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) and the question was raised as to the difference between the price of hides and the price Which the people of Canada have to pay for their footwear. Could anything be more ridiculous than the tremendous difference in price and the way in which the people of Canada are getting the worst of the deal in this respect? Can you blame the consumers of Canada for complaining when they see by the press that hog raisers in this country are getting $9.50 per hundred pounds and when they go into the different butcher shops throughout Canada they find they are charged from 50 to 60 cents a pound for ham and bacon, the same old price that the people were being charged when hogs were selling at $25. Yet the Minister of Finance asks: "What is the trouble?" Beef is 10 cents per pound on foot and yet the same old price is being charged by the abattoirs for the goods that we receive from them. Yet my hon. friend wants to know what the trouble is. Farmers who produce tobacco are receiving seven or eight cents per pound for it today and yet users of tobacco are paying the same old price for the manufactured article.
The Prime Minister, when he addressed the House on this debate the other day referred in a rather deprecating manner to the question of cream separators. Let me say for the benefit of the Prime Minister and the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) who spoke this afternoon that I drew the attention of this Parliament a number of years ago to the fact that cream separators were coming in free, and that as the hon. member for Brantford is well aware, when the Canadian manufacturers were getting out their price lists year after year, cream separators, on account of their being allowed into Canada free of duty, were the only articles on their lists that were not advanced, whereas, every pther manufactured article that was protected, was advanced in price from 10 to 25 per cent. That is the point that we wanted to convey to the people of Canada and not the matter of what cream separators are selling at on the two sides of the international boundary. The Prime Minister referred in the most complimentary

terms to Mr. Finley of the Massey-Harris Company. When he was referring to Mr. Finley's statement with respect to the cost of cream separators, with the abundant knowledge that that gentleman has of the manufacture of agricultural implements in Canada, why did he not ask Mr. Finley of that great corporation why binders and other agricultural implements are 10 per cent higher in price this year than they were in 1920, in face of the fact that wages of the labouring men in those factories have been cut at least once or twice during the last six months? Let me give this illustration by way of comparison for the benefit of the hon. member for Brantford. If a man wants to buy a binder to-day the price is $300. If he wanted to buy a binder last year, the price was in the neighbourhood of $250.
If he was going to pay for the binder last year with the oats he raised, taking the average crop as fifty bushels to the acre, it would take the crop off five acres of land, at last year's price of $1 a bushel, to pay for the binder, whereas to pay for the binder this year, taking fifty bushels to the acre, at thirty cents a bushel, which is the price oats are now selling for, it would take the crop off 20 acres to pay for that binder at present prices. That means that four times the amount of crop has to be harvested to pay for the same implement, yet the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) asks our Progressive friends, why they do not go into the manufacturing business. I say to the hon. member for Brantford: why do you not go into the farming business, if there is so much money in it?
I am glad to see the Minister of Militia in his seat. I wish to read him a short extract from his speech the other day:
Now, Mr. Speaker, we are told, on the other hand, that there will be no more war. and the cry is in some quarters: Wipe out all military expenditure. That cry is popular, very popular among some elements in this and every other country. It is particularly pleasant to the ear of the Bolshevist, to the ear of the Re I and to the crowd which gathers around the soapbox orator at the street corners in our big cities.
I wish to read another extract, which I have read on a previous occasion, to illustrate the point I am endeavouring to make. It is an extract from an article which was sent to the New York World by the present member for King's (Sir Robert Borden):
I sympathise most deeply and earnestly with every reasonable proposal for the reduction of armaments. Untold sacrifices endured in the great war will have been wholly in vain if the nations are still to compete in a mad struggle
(Mr. MoCoig.]
for supremacy in the power of destruction. The economic folly of such a policy Is too manifest to be gainsaid. Is there not a sorrowful and bitter protest from millions on the verge of starvation in Europe and which must ring in the ears of every thoughtful person.
Those are the words of the right hon. gentleman who at one time was Prime Minister of this country. I want to follow that up by referring to an article that appeared in the Toronto Globe of the very same date. It is a despatch from the city of Hamilton and is headed "Father is Sick, Kiddies Starve-Sad Case of Distress Found in a Home on Mount Hamilton." Here, right at our doors, we have a family on the verge of starvation, yet the Minister of Militia says that we have to spend millions more of the people's money to satisfy a few gentlemen in the department of which he is in charge. I say that the people of this country have no wish to rival any of the European countries in seeing how many millions of dollars they can spend on the militia. This is an agricultural country, a manufacturing country -not a military country. I want to quote a brief extract from a message that was sent to the soldiers of the Canadian Expeditionary Forces during the war, signed by the Minister of Militia:
Canada has to supply herself and the Allies with food. Men will be retained to secure the necessary production.
I believe that those words of the Minister of Militia will be received with a great deal more satisfaction by the people of this country than the message he gave to the Canadian people the other night.
Hon. gentlemen on the other side,-par- [DOT] ticularly the hon. member for Dundas (Mr. Casselman), the other night,-have made the statement and disseminated it through the press that there had been no scandals in this country since the Conservative party came into power. When I heard the hon. member for Dundas make that statement I thought that though he may be up in years, he must be young in political experience, because many hon. members now in the House will remember the binocular scandal, and the drug scandal, for his connection with which one hon. gentleman opposite was read out of the party by the Prime Minister of the day. Surely no one who is a real Canadian has forgotten these scandals, and the Allison scandal, for they were, so to speak, the most scandalous scandals we ever had in this country. Hon. members sure have not forgotten the horse scandals, and particularly the hon. member

for Dundas, because I think it was the Conservative meAiber for the county of Peel in the Provincial Legislature who was so anxious at that time to supply the demand for horses for army purposes that when he could not get horses of the desired colour, and when grey horses came along, he had them painted black so as to meet the military requirements. Surely hon. gentlemen will not forget the number of days we sat in the Public Accounts Committee listening to evidence with regard to horse scandals in the province of Nova Scotia, that little province that sends so many good men to Parliament, but which on that occasion must have slipped a cog. We all remember how thousands of dollars of the people's money wefe spent in purchasing horses that were only fit to be sold to fertilizer plants, or make mucilage to place on the Government stamps, for which there was a great demand at that time. The horse scandals in that province were so bad that the Prime Minister read out of the party the gentleman who then represented the county of King's, N.S. Yet, Mr. Speaker, we find that this gentleman, who was incapable of purchasing horses for the Government to mount, our brave boys overseas in their fight with the Hun, was selected after showing his wonderful ability as a purchasing agent for horses to be the new Superintendent of Resources, for the Canadian National railways, in Chicago-one of the most important positions in connection with our great railway system, on which we had the enormous deficit last year of $70,000,000, which the people of this country have to put up. And my hon. friend the Minister of Finance asks what is, the trouble? What is the trouble? Do you mean to say that if a man is not fit to represent a constituency in this Parliament he is able to represent the Government in one of the most important positions in connection with one of the greatest railway systems in the world? These are some of the things which are causing discontent amongst our people, and which are responsible for the demand that this Government appeal to the country so that the people may have an opportunity of expressing themselves on the question as to who shall administer the affairs of Canada.
There is another matter to which I wish to refer. The right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) the other day said that the duties on agricultural implements were lower to-day than they were when the Liberals were in power.
Let me tell my hon. friend that the request for free tractors to assist in producing greater crops in this country was first made in this Parliament by hon. gentlemen on this side of the House, and it was turned down by the Government until public opinion became so strong in favour of that measure that the Government had to grant our request and allow farm tractors to come in free.
Another important matter which was brought to the attention of Parliament by this side of the House was the question of supplying tractor ditchers. The Government at first were loathe to take action in this matter, but when the demand from the Minister of . Agriculture of every province became insistent they finally decided that it was in the interests of increased production to allow these machines, which were not manufactured in this country, to come in free of duty. But what was done? The limit was fixed at $3,000 at which they could come in free. These machines sold for $2,600 and $2,800, but the moment the price went beyond $3,000 the Government stopped their admission because they would not amend their legislation in keeping with the advanced prices of these tractor ditchers.
Now, Sir, what did the Government do during the by-election in the county of Bruce? The greatest argument they advanced was that they were looking after the interests of the farmers and were doing everything possible to further agriculture in this country. We have requested the expert of the Finance Department to increase the limit at which these tractors may come in free, and I was on the deputation with the hon. member for West Middlesex (Mr. Ross), which waited on the Minister of Agriculture and drew this matter forcibly to his attention, pointing out the importance and necessity of so amending the Act as to admit these tractor ditchers. To-day the tile factories are loaded up with tile, because they wanted to give employment to the labouring men in that industry and there is a great demand for tile drainage throughout Ontario. But the prices of these tractor ditchers are now prohibitory, as may be seen from the fact that only two of these machines were imported in 1920 and only one in 1921 from the Buckeye Tractor Company. These were both repaired machines, and were sold for less than $3,000. The importance of proper drainage is so great that the Provincial Government of Ontario, who were so greatly criticised to-day by the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt),

thought it proper to increase the loan, which they give to every farmer who wants to tile-drain his land, from $1,000 per hundred acres to $2,000. That legislation has gone into effect and the farmers availed themselves of this great privilege last year, obtaining the money necessary for this purpose, to be paid back in twenty years at 51 per cent. This Government claim that they are doing everything possible to assist the producers of this country, but they pay little attention to the requirements of the farmers. Nor do they heed the requests that are made of them from time to time. In the face of these facts, Mr. Speaker, when we find in every city and town in this great Dominion hundreds of men out of employment, and, as I said a few moments ago, families in the city of Hamilton starving; when we find dissatisfaction rampant in every province of the Dominion; and when as the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) himself states. There is nothing but trouble, I think the following lines might well be taken to heart by the Government, if they are capable of appreciating the gravity of the situation to-day:
For the debt we owe is a mighty one,
'Twill last for countless years,
For the boys who have helped to defeat the Hun
Can't be paid with cheers,
It's up to you to lend a hand 'Tis a duty none can shirk;
So wave your flags and start your bands But get these boys to work.

We have all listened with a great deal of pleasure to the stump speech of the hon. member for Kent (Mr. McCoig). That hon. gentleman, like many others who have spoken in the debate on the other side of the House, has chosen rather to make a political speech than to endeavour to contribute in some way to the solution of the great problems laid before the country by the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton). Indeed, Sir, practically the whole burden of the song on the other side has been criticism of the Militia Department, the merchant marine and the dry dock at Victoria. That, practically speaking, has been the sole contribution of many hon. members opposite to the solution of the problems with which Canada is confronted to-day. The hon. member who has just taken his seat avoided, of course, any reference to protection as it applies to tobacco, just as the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) this afternoon, in that beautiful little speech of his which was as remark- ,
able for its lack of facts as for its weakness of argument, avoided any criticism of protection of the industries in his constituency. The hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Euler) skilfully skates around the question of protection as it affects the industries in his county; and a Farmer representative last night, we found asking for protection on potatoes and pulpwood. But the great problems that are before the country have been practically passed over.
Now, what do we find? The Minister of Finance has presented a statement of the business conditions in this country which is well worthy of the earnest consideration of every member of Parliament. I do not think I am saying anything out of the way when I assert that the minister's statement has been a surprise both to the Opposition and to a great many people in the country- a surprise to the Opposition, because they did not expect such a favourable statement of the finances of Canada to-day, a statement that has left them, so far as argument is concerned, utterly helpless in discussing the Budget as presented to the House. In the statement of revenue, for the past fiscal year, which has been laid before us, we find for excise $37,000,000. That has never been questioned by any man in this House. Hon. members have not suggested that it be either added to or subtracted from. And the revenue from the Post Office, amounting to $26,000,000, has met with the same approval. The business profits tax, $40,000,000, has not been adversely criticized, and the income tax of $46,500,000 has apparently suited every one in the House. Inland revenue, amounting to $79,000,000 odd, finds no objection in any quarter, nor have the other war taxes totalling $2,355,000. The only question in the whole category that has aroused any criticism is that relating to the cqstoms revenue amounting to $163,000,000. And what have been the criticisms in that re- ' spect? Certainly no one has suggested that the revenue has been too small, and it has not been contended, either, that it is too large. It is true that statements have been made by the member for Mackenzie (Mr, Reid) and by the member for West Lamb-ton this afternoon, to the effect that an undue burden was placed upon the poorer classes of the country. Well, that statement only exemplifies one thing, and that is that these gentlemen have not taken the trouble to acquire a true knowledge of the facts.
They have not had the inclination to get the facts and certainly do not know

them. Now, Mr. Speaker, if any man will take the trouble to go through the list of items-I placed them on Hansard last year

he will ascertain that over $100,000,000 of the $170,000,000 taken in at that time was paid practically on the articles which are only bought and consumed by the wealthier people of this country. I submit that when statements are made, such as were made by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Reid), that there was a tax of $110 on every family of five in this country it shows a deplorable lack of the actual conditions as they exist in regard to the revenue. We have had some criticisms too in regard to customs duties. I followed the member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) very carefully this afternoon to find out what means of obtaining revenue he would suggest if the present method of customs duties from which we derive $165,000,000 were abolished, as my hon. friend has been advocating its abolition to a great degree. He has presented to the people of this country a number of very plausible suggestions. One was the imposition of a land tax, another direct taxation, and so on.
Mr. Speaker, I am quite certain that the people of Canada, for the time being at least, have had their fill of direct taxation. We gave them some of it last year in the form of a luxury tax, and any government that would again attempt to tax the people in that form would, in my opinion, be very unwise. Let us analyse the proposition for a moment and see what it would mean. It means this: If you are going to do away with that tax you must place taxation somewhere else, because there has been no suggestion here that any other sources of revenue than those which have been presented by the Finance Minister can be secured to carry on the affairs of the country. If you are going to raise the desired revenue by some other means what means are available? The imposition of a land tax was proposed for a while but that idea has long since been abandoned-at least I have not heard anything of it for the last twelve months. That proposition would mean a tax of $300 on every hundred-acre farm in this country. On the valuation it would mean a tax of 2| per cent. It would mean about $225 on every $5,000 farm; and if it were a head tax it would represent something like $22 for every man, woman and child in Canada. I submit there ,is no reasonable way by which the revenue which we
need can be collected so easily, and bear so lightly upon the people as by the present method. I make the assertion that this country to-day is carrying its great war debt as easily as any country in the world that was involved in the late war. It is true that we have a railroad problem, but for this I refuse to have the party on this side held responsible. When hon. members opposite first guaranteed the bonds of the Canadian Northern from Port Arthur east, they fastened, for all time to come, a railway problem upon this country as far as that road was concerned; and when they started in to build the Grand Trunk Pacific-fifty years before its time-they placed upon this country a debt and an obligation which is going to be a burden for many a day. We have been criticised by some hon. gentlemen opposite in reference to these obligations, but I am going to place those obligations where they rightly belong, and I say that those who were the means of creating them must assume the responsibility for them.
The problems before the country, as I see them, may be boiled down to two. One is that this Government has to carry on public affairs and secure enough money to pay our way as we go. The second is: what policy must be pursued in order to develop this nation in the northern part of the continent of America? As to the first,' there is no means suggested whereby the amount of money we need can be so easily raised and so lightly carried by the people as by the present method. With regard to the other question, I submit that the people of the Dominion over forty years ago settled once and for all the policy that must be pursued by Canada as long as it is a nation. That policy is the policy of protection. It was inaugurated in the year 1878, and from that time onward has never been departed from. I look upon protection as nothing more or less than an instrument for the development of the natural resources of [DOT] this country. Looking at the question from that standpoint I maintain that the policy was settled long ago-settled not only by Canada, but by the United States and almost every other country in the world-and that instrument for protection and for development is going to remain in existence as far as Canada is concerned.
I am sorry the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Claik) is not in his seat because he made some observations in his speech the other day that I would like to answer.

On that occasion he spoke about the trade of Britain increasing so rapidly. In spite of the fact that that trade has suffered a decline during the last month greater than did the trade of Canada, it is still enormous. But Mr. Speaker, he forgot to tell 

or he did not tell if he knew-that the one great cause of that trade was that nearly all the assets of the other countries of Europe are at the present time- and have been since the war-hypothecated in the Bank of England. Our Canadian manufacturers know that. They know that when they tried to give lines of credit to certain countries in Europe they were prohibited from doing so by the fact that the securities of those countries were nearly all tied up in the Bank of England, and that institution insisted that the trade should go to English traders and English manufacturers. We must bear in mind the fact that when we talk about developing our export trade with European countries it is a question of finance; and I think every man in this House will agree that as far as finance is concerned there are no better or abler people on earth than the people of the British Isles. In this connection I would like to quote a statement made by right Hon. Mr. Runciman in January, 1916, when delivering his budget. He said:
It will, in fact, be apparent to all close observers, that a country which fails to regulate and foster its industries in the national interest cannot, in the nature of things, long survive the rivalry of another country where the industries are so regulated and so fostered.
That is a statement by one of the leading men in the country which my hon. friend from Red Deer reveres so much. Let me now quote a statement by Abraham Lincoln. Ihat great statesman on one occasion said:
The tariff is a question of nation-1 housekeeping. It is to the Government what replenishing the meal tub is to the family. I
I might also quote statements from some of my hon. friend's favourite authors, such as John Stuart Mill who says, speaking of infant industries:
That a tax on infant industries for a time is the easiest way that a nation can carry them into development.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want for a few moments- and only for a few moments, for I will be brief-to place before this House some ways in which this policy has operated not only in Canada but in	the United States.
I find from statistics compiled by the Manufacturers' Association that we have

$400,000,000 of United States capital invested in this country in 600 branch factories employing no less than 87,000 men. Does any hon. member think we would have got those industries here if it had not been for our protective tariff? We have in addition $2,000,000,000 of British capital, and we have all told 700,000 hands employed in our industries. They are paying out to our people no less than $550,000,000 in wages. I ask hon. members opposite if they think that is not worth something to Canada? I would also remind them that according to the statistics our field crops in 1920 were worth $1,455,000,000. How much of that huge amount was exported? Only $271,000,000 worth. Where is their great market? The hon. member for Marquette to-day wanted to know where the manufacturer was going to sell his goods. I say to him:	If you wipe out your home
market where would the Canadian farmer sell his products? These two industries must be developed side by side to the equal benefit of both. Last year the manufacturers of this country spent $31,000,000 in wages for manufacturing food products, and employed 38,000 persons.
In that connection I want to indicate along what lines I think this country should be developed. The hon. member for Marquette this afternoon laid great stress on the American market. Unquestionably that is a great market and we would like to get into it. But how did they create that market? Did they not create it in the indentical way that I am advocating to-night? Is not the home market created by means of a protective tariff, that being the instrument which developed that enormous home market of 111,000,000 people to-day? He finds fault because we cannot get in there. Is it not natural for them to keep their market for themselves? And is it not natural for us to follow in their footsteps and create a market here along the same lines, that is, a market that they cannot take from us, which is the market that in the end will be most beneficial to Canada? Why should we hesitate to do that? Does any man doubt the ability of Canadians to do it? Compare our record in the war-I mean in a business sense. Canada with one-fifteenth of the population of the United States did one-fifth as much business. Does that indicate that we are behind them in resources or resourcefulness in developing industry and trade? It is just the opposite. I could give figures showing the enormous increase

in our foreign trade, but I will not detain the House.
The hon. member for Victoria and Carle-ton (Mr. Caldwell) the other night stated that he wanted protection on potatoes and pulpwood. I would remind him that it is only about eleven or twelve years ago since the provinces of Ontario and Quebec forbade the export of pulpwood to the American Republic. What is the result? I can show it here in a very few figures. In 1890, for example, Canada's export of pulp and paper totalled $120. I repeat the figure -$120. Last year it totalled $160,000,000. That, I contend, is the direct result of protection of that industry. In 1919 that industry employed 26,765 hands. Was it not good business to place an embargo on the export of pulpwood? Have we not created an industry in this country that is worth having and will be worth having for many years to come?
My good friend from Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) the other night presented some very interesting figures in regard to the iron and steel industry, and he will pardon me, I am sure, if I supplement them a little because it is more or less essential to my argument that I should do so. The iron and steel industry of the United States had a very severe struggle in the early days. The first attempt to introduce bessemer steel was in Milwaukee and I am told it was a failure after hundreds of millions of dollars had been invested in the enterprise. The second works were started at Troy, and I am informed that the buildings were subsequently sold for as many thousand dollars as millions were put into them. The next was the Freedom iron works in Pennsylvania, which went bankrupt, next the Vulcan steel works were started at St. Louis and failed, and following them steel mills were established at Joliette, with the same result. That is the history of the attempt to establish the iron and steel industry in the United States without suificient protection. Then the United States increased the protective duty and what happened? I do not think that I have as late figures as those presented by my hon. friend from Fort William and Rainy River, but mine are all pre-war figures, because I did not think it fair to take anything during and after the war. We are told, for example, -and I think my hon. friend's information is authoritative-that steel rails dropped from $170 to $27.50 a ton. But I am not concerned with that figure. I know it may be contended that the Bessemer
steel rails were not as good as the iron rails, that they crystallized, and so on. The point is that in 1907 there was an output of 51,000,000 tons, 56,000 workmen were employed, and they were paid $31,500,000 in wages. Was that good business for the United States or was it not?
I might also cite the plate glass industry, whose history is more or less similar. The first attempt to establish the' plate glass industry was in New Albany, Indiana, but after spending hundreds of thousands of dollars the firm went bankrupt. Next an attempt was made at Crystal City, Mexico, but it suffered the same fate. Another factory was started at Louisville, Kentucky, in 1872, and that also failed, as did a factory started at Jefferson, Indiana. Finally, sufficient protection was accorded the industry, and to-day it is one of the greatest in the United States; and incidentally the price of plate glass fell from $2.50 per square foot to 59 cents. And, Mr. Speaker, I would interject here that wherever you have a commodity controlled by an importer you always have the highest price because of lack of competition, for it is competition within your own country that brings down prices and gives you cheaper goods.
Then take the pineapple industry in the United States, the history of which will be of interest to our farmer friends. The industry is just developing, but before a duty was placed on pineapples only 100000 crates were grown in the United States; in ten years that production has increased to over 1,000,000 crates. The same thing happened in respect to the wire nail industry. Prior to 1883 there was a tariff on wire nails of one cent a pound; they were selling at 7 and 8 cents a pound, and were practically all imported. In 1900 the duty was doubled, 5,000,000 kegs were made in the United States and the price dropped to 2 cents. The same happened in respect to sugar. When the Dingley tariff was passed in 1897 there were only six sugar factories in the United States, and the output was only 37,500 tons. In 1910 there were 65 factories and over 400,000 tons were produced annually; there was a fixed investment of $100,000,000 in the industry and $40,000,000 was paid out to the farmers and the labour employed in connection with it. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, if that is not the kind of industry that is worth something to a country? In ten years the United States sugar factories produced 24,245,000 tons of sugar and paid $121,000,000 in wages.

I repeat, I am sorry the hon. member for Red Deer is not in his seat because I have some other figures that I should like to call to his attention, but it is not worth while putting them on Hansard. My point is that from the time Great Britain inaugurated free trade until the present time, her exports to protected countries have been diminishing year after year and her imports from the same countries have been increasing. We know that she had an adverse balance of trade, but there is more than that in the matter. If you would subtract from her adverse balance of trade, her trade with her colonies and countries without a protective tariff, you would find that the showing would be still worse. She made up her loss to protected countries 'by increasing her trade with her colonies and countries without a protective tariff. Let me carry the argument a little further. If all these countries protect themselves against her, it can be readily seen how Great Britain is going to be handicapped in trade, and I do not wonder that, at the present time, she is rapidly drifting towards protection. I have a great deal of admiration for the people of Great Britain; I think they are the best and most resourceful people on earth; I am not a prophet, but I do not think it will be many years before free trade in England will be a thing of the past. I think it was Chamberlain who said that "a nation that ties its hands, gets pretty well cuffed." The hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) said the other night:	"She loses

Before I close, I want to point out that even Great Britain developed her industrial conditions under protection. When she threw away protection in 1849, she was the most highly developed industrial country in the world, and, consequently, she was capable, not only of looking after herself, but of getting a great deal of the business of the world. I should like to refer for a few moments to our former friends and see what we have done for them. I will not refer to the reduction which this Government has made for their benefit in agricultural implements. It is not necessary for me to refer to the list of expenditures that we have, running into millions every year, on agriculture, and in my opinion, more should be spent. But when they object, as they did the other night, to giving Roumania a

I only wish that could be done again this year. I do not think it is fair to advocate protection in one direction unless you carry

it all along the line. I am firmly convinced that, in protection, -we have the only instrument that can make Canada a great country, and in that regard I include protection for the farmer as well as for every other man. I can quite readily see the rationality of the United States in trying to protect the farmers of that country. That has been the principle of the Republican party since that party was formed, and there is not a man in this House who does not know that, if the Young Bill goes through, it is going to be a detriment to Canada, but at the same time it is going to be a help to the farmers of the United States. The idea is that they want to protect their industries, their farmers and everything else within the borders of their country. That is the policy that should be carried out in this country.

the future. I believe Canada, with her immense natural resources of all kinds, must develop and perfect them to the greatest degree within her o\vn borders, and that we must send out from this country the finished product, thus giving the greatest benefit to the present number of our people.

(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, the Budget speech is always interesting to this House and to the people of this country; but it is more so this year because the speech from the Throne announced that there would be a revision of the tariff during the present session. However, on the 9th instant the hon. Minister of Finance declared that the revision of the tariff would not take place this year. Now, the Government had judged proper during last year to appoint a commission composed of ministers and secretaries, to go over the country from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and inquire into our needs and guide the hon. Minister of Finance in this tariff revision. To my mind there was no need of this commission going over the country and spending tens and tens of thousands of dollars if the Government had no intention of going on with this revision. But I am not surprised, Mr. Speaker, that there should be no revision this year, for I have somewhat followed the right hon. Prime Minister's round last fall, and I concluded from his speeches that he did not want a tariff revision, for everywhere he preached the protection policy inaugurated in 1878. He contended in his speeches that it was the only proper one for the country. It was therefore useless to have spent the people's money on this errand.
Before entering upon the consideration which I intend to offer upon the new taxation, I must say that I do not very heartily endorse the new liabilities, for I did not encourage the Imperialistic policy which has been carried on since 1914. I was for three years the only one in this House to protest against this insane policy of sending five or six hundred thousand men to the great European war. I will recall to you, Mr. Speaker, what I stood for in this House in 1915. I then stated that we should take part in this war, but according to our means. I gave the illustration of a son who must help his father; but I added that if both were threatened with ruin, the son should stand aloof, for with a young family to bring up he should save the little money he has. The reverse took place, Mr. Speaker, we enlisted 590,000 soldiers, and

the result is that the son is ruined while the father is enabled to decrease the amount of his debts. Such is the result of our participation in the war. I see in the public reports that England has in the course of the fiscal year just ended decreased its debt by more than one thousand million dollars, while we have increased ours by more than hundred and one millions. If my opinion had been listened to at the time, if the Government of the day, led by the right hon. member for King's (Sir Robert Borden) had understood the interest of the country, they would have realized that the interest of the country would not permit the sending of more than one hundred thousand men, for instance, I will say two hundred thousand men in deference to the Imperialists. I believe that any nation in Enrope would have been satisfied with this contribution, for at that time neither England nor France, nor the other Allies, expected more from Canada, as it was known we could not do better.
In order to prove that I was right at that time, and that 200,000 men were a sufficient sacrifice-it was even too much, to my mind, but I allow this figure in order not to arouse the warriors of this House-here is what I find in the report of the proceedings of the special committee appointed by a resolution of the House of Commons, of September 18, 1919, to which was referred Bill No. 10 to amend the Act creating a Department for the re-establishment of returned soldiers in civil life, as well as certain Orders in Council relating to the work of that department:

Now, Mr. Speaker, what conclusion could an impartial man draw from all this-I mean a man who is not a politician, who is biased by no political considerations? It is this, that when the Government whose leader was the right hon. member for King's (Sir Robert Borden) imposed upon us as a conscription of 100;000 men, it was not with the object of winning the war, but of winning the election of 1917. If there were an immediate need of 100,000 men, why did the Prime Minister and the Minister of Militia not send first the 50,000 men who were in England at that time and the 50,000 men who were here in Canada and whom the Government kept here to hunt for conscripts through the country? That would have solved the problem of the 100,000 men alleged to be needed. But that did not suit the Government. Conscription was imposed. What happened? The available soldiers in Canada were used to gather conscripts. The province of Quebec was hounded. The object of conscription was to win the election. The Government wanted to have it said in the other provinces that it was absolutely necessary to enforce conscription against the Quebec people who refused to do their duty. Our friends from Ontario were nevertheless a little disappointed themselves, for their candidates had promised them that they would not be disturbed by conscrip-

The hon. minister will tell you that with the ordinary revenue he has been able to pay the ordinary and the extraordinary expenses. I hold that the revenue which the minister to-day calls an ordinary one, is really one drawn from extraordinary sources, seeing that every year new taxes are added; the $135,000,000 of war tax in 1919-1920 hav-[Mr. RanetOt-I

Minister of Finance will again declare before this House and the country: 'With the ordinary revenue, I have paid up both the current and unusual expenses," but what he has not mentioned is that he has collected $300,000,000 in war tax, since 1917; these did not exist before 1914.
But this is not all, Mr. Speaker. Take for instance the custom duties in 19191920 and 1920-1921. In 1920, it amounted to $167,000,000 and in 1921, it was $163,000,000; while before the war we had a revenue of $70,000,000. Why the difference? Is it owing to the increase of our population, if within the last six years our revenue has more than doubled? No, Sir, the reason will be found in the higher price we have paid for goods that have been bought since the war. In many cases the duties are paid ad valorem according to the value of the merchandise and these having tripled in value in many instances, the duties are three times as high. As an example, a piece of cloth, let us say a web of 100 yards at $1.40 per yard = $140 at 30 per cent duty=$42. Let us suppose that the same cloth had been bought in 1914, a web of 100 yards, exactly the same quantity-but the quality is not the same -these goods have trebled and even increased fourfold in price in many cases. As a base of comparison let us say it has increased three times, it is therefore no more 100 yards of cloth at $1.40 but at $4.20 which gives $420 at 30 per cent ad valorem=$126 which brings to the public treasury three times as much money. The minister is well acquainted with this fact, that the custom duties for the year 19211922 amount to $135,000,000 in comparison with $163,000,000 which they amounted to last year, not that our population is less than last year, but for the simple reason that goods we now buy have come down in price.

If such is the case, Sir, our people have thus paid, from 1915 up to this day, on an average more than double what they paid before the war, therefore, we have not only had war taxes bringing in an extraordinary revenue, but also from 60 to 80 million dollars in custom duties as an extraordinary revenue. Add these figures to the war taxes and you arrive to conclusion that this year we have paid very closely to $300,000,000 in new taxes, and that we shall be paying very near to $350,000,000 in 1921-1922. Mr. Speaker, the minister will tell us, that things were well done; but is it not a fact that the people played their part also? Shall we be better off next year? No, Sir, we shall be in a worse position owing to this further taxation. By this exportation and importation tax of li to 3 per cent and of 2i to 4 per cent, the hon. Minister of Finance will no doubt collect a large amount of money, because every one is called upon to pay, the poor even more than the rich. I have often heard remarks on the part of my good Montreal friends, which I could not endorse, with reference to the agricultural class not paying any income tax neither the higher paid artisans and that invariably the tax falls on the capitalist. I differ in opinion with them. The wholesale merchant of Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg or of anywhere else, who carries on a large business from which he derives large profits, certainly pays a large amount as an income tax; but that same merchant figures out first his expenses, before setting a price on his goods, and I am sure that he does not omit his rent, if he is a tenant, his municipal taxes, his staff and lastly his income tax, whether it be $50,000 or $100,000 and in the end we find that it is the people who pay.
