He gives us the following figures: Ordinary expenditures, $343, 021,594; capital expenditure, $27,459,127; demobilization, $7,777,380, making a total of $378,258,101. I have nothing ito say against ordinary expenditures, unless for instance we iShouild certainly economizlei *something as regards to public works. This year we might save from twelve to fifteen million dollars on works Which are not urgent and which mostly have been promised at election time in order to return either a minister or a member supporting the Government.
It is not worth the price.

It is too expensive. We might also economize ion the Militia of my old and esteemed friend the Minister of Militia (Mr. Guthrie). I have always strongly protested in this House against this folly of militarism in our country. When my hom. tfirienld the Minister of Militia asks the House to vote his militia estimates he goes into comparisons, he talks about our sister Dominions, he takes us to Europe, even to Asia and Africa and he concludes by stating that we are the only country in the world spending so little for her army. The hon. minister forgets to state that geographically we are so situated that we could cease (spending any more money for army purposes and that the other British colonies are not in a similar situation. This is why I think that not a cent should be spent for the next five years, but I am ready to allow a few military expenses so as to satisfy my imperialistic friends. This year we are spending twelve millions for the Militia. Why not cut this amount in half and spend only six millions.
That's too much.

One of the hon. member says it is too much. Quite true, it is too much in my opinion, but I wanted to make suggestions to the Government although I am perfectly 'convinced they will not accept them. Does the hon. Minister

of Militia claim that at the present time it is absolutely necessary to give to a number of our young men a military training? Will the hon. minister state that it is absolutely necessary for us to have soldiers? Why? In case another war should take place in Europe is there a 'Government at Ottawa willing to throw us in that new war when we are practically ruined? For my part I would not send another single soldier in Europe to take part in another war. Was not our war against Prussians also directed against militarism which we wanted to destroy in the world? Now that we have the League of Nations some of our political men claint that our status is changed, that we have a different standing from what we had before the war. It is true that our 'status is changed, when we have to pay as well as the great European powers, but when it comes to receive, we shall revert to our colonial status, we 'shall be told that Downing Street still governs us and we will not get a cent of the war indemnity. We are mighty important people when it is a question of paying out but when there shlal be something to 'collect, we will -be assigned a back seat and we will not get a red cent.
But, that is not all. We have also an air fleet, so they say, which will cost $1,625,000 this year. Why should we have an air fleet at the present time? I fail to understand why we go on with such folies. If our forefathers could come back and were told that we are 'spending so much on militarism, they would say: What is the world becoming? In my opinion not a cent should 'be spent for such purposes and in this way we could save the country this amount of $1,625,000. I only wish we did not spend a dollar for that air fleet because we might thus save the country an expenditure of $1,625,000.
The hon. Minister of Militia says that the Mounted Police do not come under his jurisdiction, but I suppose there is a member of the Government Who has charge of this department and I must tell him just now, that it is shocking to see the Mounted Police parading the streets in Ottawa.
I have been here for 17 years, and I consider that the city of Ottawa does not need the Mounted Police f parading the streets. Ottawa is one of the most peaceful cities in the country, and therefore there is no necessity of keeping the Mounted Police here. That is why I say to the Government, with regard to this credit: You have about four million dollars, you may easily cut out two million and a half.

And that is not all. The hon. Minister of Marine has obtained for us a gift of three ships from the Mother Country- England. The upkeep of this present is quite expensive. The crew must be fed and paid and1 we must buy coal. This involves considerable expenditure. Under the circumstances, I would suggest that the minister place his gift in safety at Montreal, at the million dollar island, for example, or elsewhere, and leave It there for five years, so that we may save the country at least two million dollars a year, which would mean a saving of ten millions.
I am economical myself, I preach and practice economy, and if my hon. friends did the same, it would be to the greater benefit and happiness of the people.
The hon. Minister of Finance spoke the other day of non-productive investments, that is to say, which do not yield any returns. Where I come from we know nothing of this kind of investment. He mentioned the following:
C.N.R. Railway	$ 50,000,009
Grand Trunk	 89,687,633
Grand Trunk Pacific	 26,000,000
Total	$165,687,633
He told us that certain amounts should be charged to current expenditure of the year, 'but that he could not do it this year as there is already a large deficit, although he said at first that he had a surplus of 12 million dollars which subsequently was absorbed by a deficit. I must say that, so far as it concerns the railway question in which all Canada is interested, and particularly those who use them, who have goods to ship from one end of the country to the other, that there practically exists an embargo, at the present time, on the shipment of our goods. For several reasons, this railway policy has been disastious to the people of this country; all politicians are more or less responsible for that. The hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. Davidson) began just now to discuss the question but he stopped suddenly. I have already had the occasion, during the session, to speak of railways; however, I wish to speak further on the subject. The party which is now in power is the same as in 1911, although it has changed its name.
An alias.

(Translation.) But the staff is the same. Some are dead, others have resigned, but it is still the Conservative party

call it what you will-it is the

party which has advocated this railway policy from 1911 until now.
The Prime Minister has frequently told us that the Liberal party were responsible for the present situation; that Sir Wilfrid Laurier's railway policy had been disastrous, and that the Liberal party wanted to wash their hands of this, claiming they were not responsible. I say that those who are most guilty are the present leaders of the Government. If Sir Wilfrid Laurier's policy was not good in 1911, why have you continued such a policy? If the railway construction from Port Arthur to Montreal was of no advantage to the people of this country, why, after the elections of 1911, did you continue it, with Mackenzie and Mann, and why, later, did you extend the Canadian Northern railway from the prairies to Vancouver. Is it our fault if we now have three transcontinental railways to go to the Pacific ocean? It has been the most disastrous policy which a Government could have adopted. But, what could have been done at the time-I blame both parties for this-what should have been done in 1911 would have been not to give 35 million dollars to Mackenzie and Mann, but to expropriate them and to settle with them once for all as early as 1911, and to use these branch-lines in the West as "feeders" for the Transcontinental National and then the Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific would have been a success. The Government of the day was not interested to make the Grand Trunk Padific a success, but the new Government whose leader was the right hon. member for King's (N.S.) (Sir Robert Borden), from the very moment they came into power, in 1911, endeavoured to destroy Sir Wilfrid Laurier's work. They did all they could; they made an investigation and some enthusiastic supporters of this Government endeavoured to disparage as much as possible Sir Wilfrid Laurier's undertaking, and to prevent the Grand Trunk from taking control of it. That is what that party has done. They committed a serious offence, when, for political purposes, they disparaged the property of the people of this country.
Slanderers.

'rtiey were slanderers. It is awful for a party to destroy, simply for political purposes, property which cost $171,000,000. I say, Mr. Speaker, that a party holding such conduct will be severely punished in due
time. Is there a Government in a country like ours who are able to administer the railways, and particularly this Government who never made a success of any of their undertakings? For instance, they gave out contracts three years in advance and sometimes at a much higher price than was warranted. Just think, they under look to operate in accordance with what was being done in the United States the railways of this country, whose area is equal to that of. the United States, but whose population is only 8J millions, compared with 105 millions in the neighbouring Republic, then to apply here the eight hour day, according to the McAdoo schedule; and the result is that we have throughout the country many railways paralleling one another. Please notice what is being done here in the capital. There are twelve trains leaving Ottawa for Montreal every day, and the same number going in the opposite way, which makes twenty four trains daily.
I have a suggestion to make with a view to preventing our railway policy to ruin the country. I think the Government did not take the trouble to read the memorandum addressed to them by Lord Shaughnessy. As far as I am concerned, I have a right to speak in the name of the 234th part of this country, since we are 234 members of Parliament. Well, in my opinion, the sooner we get rid of our national railways, the better it will be; and personaly, I say very frankly that I am not very particular about the way in which we may get rid of them: Be it for one, of for five, or for one million dollars, I would get rid of them immediately. I would not confide the operation of our railways to a company like Mackenzie and Mann, but to a company like the Canadian Pacific, administered by a board of directors possessed of great experience. Then you would see a great change in the administration at the end of four or five years, and instead of having deficit upon deficit, we might have a surplus. But can you ever expect any return on a railway administered by a so-called independent board, for they contend that the Civil Service Commission is an independent body and that patronage has been abolished. But the Government is doing nothing without patronage. I shall refer to it later. For the moment, I am dealing with our railways and the way to ensure their effective operation. Whom do you see at the head of those railways? Mr. Hanna and Sir Hormisdas Laporte. What does Sir

Hormidas Laporte know about railways? He knows all about sugar and molasses, but absolutely nothing about railways. However they are the men who are expected to administer with profit our 17,000 miles of national railways.
Now we have the Grand Trunk on our hands. That company seems to be very fastidious; they will not accept the views of the Government nor the results of the arbitration. I would like to be the party to decide and I would soon settle their case; I would refuse to take control of that railway and I am sure people would approve of my decision. But this Government want to have the Grand Trunk; they want everything in the world, and then we shall have to pay for it. But what shall we pay with? The hon. Minister of Finance will impose some new taxes, and more taxes all the time.
The Government is responsible for this railway policy which is bearing so heavily on the people of this country. You might just as well say to the Government that there are dealers to-day who have very large stocks and who are in financial straits. Personally, as a hay merchant, I have lost money and I am going to lose some more. Why don't you help me out? The railway companies need but' to apply to the Government. The very men who led those railways to bankruptcy are still the advisers of the roads. Mackenzie and Mann are there, behind the screens, working in behalf of this Government. There is one thing that is always tempting all political, parties and it was the misfortune of many a country in the world:	The
elections are drawing near, and they often come sooner that it is desired.
There are two openings now; these elections were not wanted, but unfortunately, the representatives of these ridings died.
I understand that the Government require a lot of money for that; the big railway men are asked to contribute and thousands, nay, hundreds of thousands of dollars are secured in that way for electoral purposes. Later on, you cannot refuse to do a good turn to these gentlemen should they be embarrassed, and the people have to foot the Bill. I congratulate my friends of the Agrarian party for having adopted a better method, that of having the campaign funds voted by the riding which is to elect a representative. What I have found to be the best system is to work in the interest of my constituents, to tell the truth, to say whether such legislation is good or bad and when it is bad, to vote against it. Then I

go back to my constituency where I can be elected without disbursing a red cent.
The hon. Minister of Finance in his Budget speech, gave us the net debt of this country, but not our total of indebtedness. I looked in the Official Gazette and there I saw that the gross debt, of this country in March last, amounted to $3,000,000,000. I was particularly impressed by the amount of interest which we are paying on our debt and which amounts to almost $143,000,000. If our obligations were only $2,350,000,000, we would not be paying such a large amount of interest. Now I have always held and I still hold that the actual debt is represented by the total amount of our indebtedness, because we are not sure of getting back the amounts due to us which we include as assets. The Government has advanced money to foreign countries upon which it receives no interest and there are many loans, out of which we get no returns. Therefore I say that our debt amounts not only to $2,350,000,000, but reaches $3,000,000,000, and I am going to prove it. We are paying this year $142,000,000 for interest, that is an increase of $519,069.69 over last year. Our deficit of $101,000,000 for last year, will increase by so much our interests for 192223. It means that within two or three years we shall have to pay $150,000,000 for interests. Moreover, our railways do not pay their operating charges. We have to borrow and add that to capital.
If we maintain that railway policy, in five years from now, our debt will not only amount to $3,000,000,000, but judging by what our railways have cost us up to now -except the Grand Trunk-I do not think I am misleading the House in saying that we shall owe $1,000,000,000, for our railways alone. Three billions and one billion, make four billion dollars, and if we acquire the Grand Trunk which will cost, I suppose, four or five hundred million dollars and perhaps a good deal more, in five years, our total debt will certainly amount to $5,000,000,000. Therefore I say to you: What shall we become with such an enormous debt, and why should we have it? We owe it to our war-time folly, to our foolish acquisition of bankrupt railways, and also to the fact that we have adopted the McAdoo schedule. Again I ask you: Whj^ should we have adopted the eight-hour day for our railway employees? Today conductors and engineers earn more than professional men in the country districts. Some conductors are earning as much as $5,500, others $4,500 and $4,000.
Per month.

No, per year. Is there any reason why, to-day, after the war, and poor as we are, we should maintain the eight-hour day? Not at all, Mr. Speaker. Let us come back to pre-war conditions and let us establish a ten-hour day for all railway employees. An eight-hour day is sufficient for men who are working in factories and mines, but for railway employees as well as for us farmers, a ten-hour working day does no harm. It is a well known fact that railway employees, whether on our national roads or on the Canadian Pacific railway, are not working only eight hours a day, but in many cases, sixteen and eighteen hours, in other to get time and a half. Under such conditions it is very hard to come out even.
I was saying a moment ago that I was surprised to see in the Estimates such large provisions for demobilization. The armistice was signed nearly three years ago and yet this Parliament is asked to vote seven or eight million dollars for the purpose of demobilization. I think that it is simply a pretext given by the Government to take better care of their friends, and we have a proof in that certain lawyers in Winnipeg have been well oared for, not so very long ago, out of those demobilization Estimates. Somebody assured me that a law firm in Winnipeg, drew the small amount of $56,000 for 102 days of work. This, I admit, was unsatisfactory to other firms in that city, so they had to retain the services of other lawyers in order to do away with all bitterness. The Department of Justice did that, they took in some other lawyers and, as stated before the Committee on Public Accounts a few days ago, $180,000 were paid to lawyers in Winnipeg to secure the punishment of workingmen who had indulged in seditious appeals during the Winnipeg strike, it was found necessary to hire the help of lawyers in order to have those people imprisoned. Mr. Speaker, I protest against this fraudulent appropriation of the money voted by this House for a special purpose and not with the intention of feeding any Winnipeg lawyers in spite of the well-known fact that some ten odd lawyers are to be found in the offices of the Department of Justice at Ottawa. Of course, many lawyers are required there, as the Minister of Justice can devote but a small part of his time to the business, for the reason that he is too busy outside, having estates to manage, banks to take
care of as director, too many "jobs," as our good Canadians say. He wants some help, and so much the more so as he is. advanced in years and suffering from illness. Then, he has to keep tab of all his salaries, the amount of his pension, of his investments; this also requires a good deal of time and, therefore, there must be a good many lawyers at work in his department. I am told that there are ten. Why not take two, for instance, and send them where trouble happens to arise. Instead of paying $56,000 to outside lawyers one might have relieved the congestion in the Department of Justice and left there a staff of eight. I do not suppose that a business man, a hay dealer or a wholesale dealer in Montreal would apply to a lawyer in Ottawa with respect to a case he had to plead in this city if he had already retained the services of another lawyer with respect to his general business. I can safely say that the Government would save at least $500,000 a year by resorting to the services of the lawyers whom they have already engaged, and permanently so, at Ottawa, and by leaving the outside lawyers with their own business. I am pretty sure that everything would be carried on to the best advantage in this way. The right hon. Prime Minister has inquired, on many occasions, what was the stand of the Opposition as regards the tariff question, stating that the next election would be fought on that mere question. Speaking for myself only, I must tell the Prime Minister right away, that as far as I am concerned and as far as the county of Laprairie-Napierville is concerned, he will have some other questions to settle with me and with my electors if, as I hope, we are to have an election shortly. The Prime Minister must be judged on what he has done to date. If he has sinned he must be punished. The man who dies to-day will not be punished for the faults which he might have committed twenty years from now, but for the faults committed in the past. I merely want the Prime Minister to be punished for the sins he has committed and not for those which he might commit in the future. The farmers in our counties know a tree by its fruit. "The tree which bears no good fruit shall be cut and cast into the fire." Of course, I would not tell my electors to sentence the Prime Minister to be thrown in the fire, but I shall have him condemned to go back to the Opposition side, that is the only punishment I wish him.

As far as I am concerned, I would like to discuss the treatment which we have received at the hands of the Prime Minister. I remember that, on several occasions, we have been charged by hon. gentlemen opposite with being cowards and slackers. Well, let me tell the Prime Minister right now, that he will find the electors of my county to be no cowards and that they will go to the polling booths and deposit their ballots in the ballot boxes, but not in his favour. The right hon. Prime Minister will leave for Europe shortly, in order to attend the Imperial conference. I look unfavourably on his departure, but, after all, the majority of the House has authorized it. I am very much afraid he will come back to this country with new obligations imposed upon the Canadian people, although he will have received no mandate aforehand to bind the country; but, anyhow, this House has given him carte blanche.

(Translation.) On

(Translation.) . . . on division. I am not sending him, nor is my hon. friend from Nicolet (Mr. Trahan). However, he will leave shortly. I suppose he will be wise enough not to take an unseaworthy boat. I hope he will take a seaworthy boat so as to get overseas safely; he will make a good choice and I approve him. But when he taunts the members of the Agrarian party for selecting their boat and getting in ours, being unwilling to risk themselves in the Government's leaky craft, then I disapprove him. I want him to leave on a good boat that he may sail safely, but I want him also to let others have their own say in choosing a craft for themselves.

speakeroldname: Mr. R. H. BUTTS (Cape Breton South and Richmond):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Budget speeeh has taken a most peculiar turn in the remarks of the hon. gentleman who has just preceded me (Mr. Lanctot). He talked about everything except what his own side of the House have been talking about since this debate began. Surely the platform they have adopted since this debate has been in progress was wide enough to admit my hon. friend, for it included all kinds of fantastic economic theories. My hon. friend, however, has chosen to confine his remarks to railway matters and naval affairs, and he never even touched on the question of pressed hay, in which I understand he is very much interested.

I have followed with a great deal of attention the speeches delivered on both sides of the House, and the difference between the two sides is really quite marked. I do not think anybody with any degree of reason whatever could have any doubt_ as to the policy of hon. members who sit to your right, Mr. Speaker. I do not think there is need for anything further to be said as to our attitude on this side of the House after the speech of the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen). The policy outlined by him is, I believe, unanimously supported by hon. members on this side of the House. But when we turn to the other side we find the greatest medley of economic inconsistencies that could possibly be conceived of. Take, for instance, my hon. friend from North Cape Breton and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie). When leader of the Opposition he laid down a fiscal policy; it is there crystallized in Hansard for all time. He said:
No, while we may have iron and steel in the raw state in this country, there may be others who can pour their products into this country and keep us forever from having an industry of that kind for our own. If I were to say that, and to allow the natural resources of this country to remain forever in a dormant state, I do not consider that I would be doing what would be in the best interests of my country or for the general advancement of the people. If to take some specific object of that kind and to provide for it in the way in which I think it should be provided for its Toryism, or protectionism, or unreasonable, as regards the general trade of the country, I must plead guilty.
That is a very clear definition of where he stands, and certainly it is good, sound protectionist doctrine. I understand that my hon. friend has since very humbly apologized for his stand on that occasion. I am told he has said he then made a mistake, and I am quite prepared to believe that, for in this Parliament on more than one occasion he has said he was not a protectionist, but that he was in favour of bounties. Now if there is any vice in protection, in bounties you have the most vicious type of protection.
Coming to my hon. friend from Maison-neuve and Gaspe (Mr. Lemieux), who sits next, he is the greatest protectionist in all Quebec when he is in the constituency of Maisonneuve, but when in Gaspe, in his advocacy of free trade he is only rivalled by my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr Clark).
Coming down a bit further to the hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), he is all things to all constituencies.

It makes no difference what constituency he is in, he has a coat that will fit it.
Coming now to the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), I can remember, though it is quite a few years ago, hearing him deliver a speech in the city of Sydney, right in the centre of the coal fields of Cape Breton, in which he said that if the coal trade of Nova Scotia could not stand without protection, then let it fall. Here in this House, a few nights ago, he told us that he was not a free trader, and never had been.
Coming now to my imaginative friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster), at the Liberal convention here in Ottawa, he said: Yes I am a free trader, but in theory only. My imaginative friend imagines he is a free trader, but I do not think there is any one in this House imaginative enough to imagine for one moment that he does anything more than imagine he is a free trader. He is not one in reality.
Coming now to my hon. friend from Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon), after talking along protectionist lines all night he turned round at the heel of the hunt and said that tariff for revenue was good, but no tariff at all was better, and then sat down, so we did not know which side of the fence he was on. He left us in doubt as to his position, on the tariff.
My hon. friend from Victoria and Carle-ton (Mr. Caldwell) is, of course, an out and out free trader. He was a free trader in potatoes and farm products all during the war when he was getting $4 and $5 a bushel, but now that this new tariff has come into effect in the United States and closed, him out, he is no longer a free trader. He is a protectionist now, and he wants the Canadian Government to rstain the Canadian market, not only for potatoes, but for farm products generally. He would welcome an expert duty on pulpwood. So you see his is a brand-new type of protection, different altogether from that advocated by hon. gentlemen who sit on the front benches on this side.
My hon. friend from Queen's (Mr. Sinclair) is in favour of an altogether different type of protection. He talks neither free trade nor protection, but under some kind of a veil he advocates a new species of protection that I never heard of before. He tells us that in Prince Edward Island they cannot sell potatoes at 17 cents. Now potatoes were on the free list up till very recently, but when the American tariff is put on, my hon. friend runs for cover, and
seeks protection of a very peculiar type. He wants this Government to reduce the freight rates on potatoes from Prince Edward Island by about two-thirds for several months, and I suppose later on he will not need so much protection. It is not strange, therefore, that I should call this a medley of economic contradictions. Turn it what way you will, the most you can possibly make of it is that they cling to that old phanton of free trade, while in reality they are protectionists of one kind or another, save only my imaginative and hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) and my hon. friend from Bed Deer (Mr. Clark), who hold to that old phanton, and who are the only remaining examples of an almost extinct species.
Now, let us just look very briefly over the fiscal policy of this country, as far back as you wish to go. You will find that when protection was adopted four or five hundred miles of railroads were all that we had in the Dominion, and under the protectionist policy which has obtained from 1878 until to-day, this Dominion, with a population varying from, at that time, five and a half millions or six millions to eight or liine millions to-day, has built forty thousand miles of railway. To-day, although perhaps we should be better off without some of the railways, the Dominion of Canada has a greater mileage of railroads per capita than any other country in the world, and they have been built under protection. Previous to 1911 we had spent approximately $250,000,000 on a canal system, opening up a waterway from the mouth of the St. Lawrence 2,500 miles into the interior of this country; and that was built under protection.
When hon. gentlemen opposite were in opposition previous to 1896 they yelled free trade, so that the capitalists did place some amount of credence in their declarations. They thought that after the preaching of years, surely the Liberal party would do something to bring about a lower tariff, and for that very reason, during those years, there was something unstable in the commercial conditions of Canada. But when in 1897 the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) brought down a protectionist Budget and further stabilized the trade of Canada, then it was that the capitalists began to feel confidence in the resources of this country; and during the ten years that followed there came into Canada $300,000,000 of American money to build up factories and develop the resources of the

Dominion. It was realized then that there was no longer a dispute between the protectionists and the free traders. The American capitalists began to realize that we were all of one fold, with one shepherd; we were all protectionists; hence the stability of trade, hence the influx of capital, hence the golden age which my hon. friend from Maisonneuve and Gaspe (Mr. Lemieux) has spoken of. Can he expect any one to believe that it was their political doctrines that brought about the age of prosperiy that lasted from the time when our fiscal policy and our trade conditions were stabilized, right down to the beginning of the war? I do not think he will seriously contend anything of the kind. It is true that if they did not raise the tariff of their predecessors, neither did they make any attempt to cut it down as it stood when they came into power.
Let me look for a moment at the condition of our foreign trade under protection. In 1866 our foreign trade amounted to $131,000,000, including imports and exports; in 1890 it was $218,000,000; but by 1900-from 1890 to 1900 were protectionist years-we increased our foreign trade from $218,000,000 to $693,000,000. We did that under protection. The home interchanges in Canada in 1911 amounted to $1,000,000,000 and the yearly wages paid out in Canada at that time amounted to $250,000,000. These are some of the figures that make us pause and consider; these are the conditions that made the Laurier Government also pause and think, and that prompted the member for Shelburne and Queen's, who was formerly Minister of Finance, to throw to the winds those whimsical ideas he entertained while in Opposition, when he felt no responsibility whatever upon his shoulders, and to adopt the policy that had proven itself in the country, the policy of wiser statesmen than he. That hon. gentleman's wisdom consisted principally in knowing enough about the tariff to be guided by those who were more conversant with the situation than he was.
Well, time went on and my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's could not get clear of that little hobby horse of his younger days; and the time came when he and the late Hon. William * Paterson went down to Washington to negotiate the Reciprocity Pact. Now, I have read a good portion of the book of life, and I have read a few more books, and I have learned from them that one very strong criterion of truth is public opinion. If that is so, then I say that the criterion of truth in

all of Canada's days has been against the idea of free trade, or even of a low tariff. When that pact was negotiated, the very first thing we knew in Canada was that the legislatures of British Columbia, Manitoba, Ontario and New Brunswick passed resolutions opposing it. Nova Scotia and Saskatchewan approved of it; the provinces of Ontario and New Brunswick legislated against it. Pulp-wood and timber cut on Crown and leased lands were not allowed to be exported to the United States. So you see the provinces of British Columbia, Manitoba, Ontario and New Brunswick, through their legislatures, protested against this pact. Let me just reiterate the words "that public opinion is a very strong criterion of truth." If it is, and we are guided by it, then we must say that a fair, moderate, and just protection to our industries is what the people of Canada wish for and what they will have retained.
I wish now to make a few remarks upon our steel trade. I am not going to speaK of the coal trade to-night. I do not think it would be appropriate for me to do so because there is a special committee now considering that very question. They are taking evidence but they have, as yet, made no report and anything that I might say now would at least be characterized as inopportune. I shall, however, speak briefly upon the iron and steel industry. Now if we follow the history of that industry in the United States, with respect to the tariff conditions that have prevailed, we will find that the production of pig iron in the adjoining republic has assumed enormous proportions and developed to its present position under a high tariff. In 1868, when the industry was in its infancy, a tariff of $9 per ton was placed upon |pig iron, This tariff was in 1874 reduced to $7 per ton, at which figure it remained until 1887 when it was further reduced to $6.72 per ton. In 1894 the tariff was further reduced to $4, at which figure it remained until 1910 when a reduction to $2.50 per ton was made. In the meantime, and as a result of the protection that it had received under that tariff, the pig iron industry of the United States had grown to such enormous proportions that the duty "was entirely removed. Pig iron was put on the free list, and that product in the United States competed with all the countries of the world. The development of the industry was so immense that it was

able, and more than able, to engage in such competition.
Take steel ingots and billets. The manufacture of steel ingots and billets in the United States was developed under similar circumstances. The tariff on certain grades of ingots and billets in 1868 varied from $25 to $70 per ton. The tariff was reduced by 10 per cent in 1874, but this reduction was afterwards eliminated in 1879. In 1894 there was a further reduction when the tariff varied, according to the quality of steel, from $5.36 to $83.90 per ton. The tariff was greater in 1894 on steel billets in the United States than they could be sold for to-day, not speaking of duty at all. Later on, under that tariff, the time came when they were able to make those products duty free, the steel industry having increased to such enormous proportions. The same is true in regard to wire rods, the manufacture of which received similar encouragement. In 1868 a tariff of $30 a ton was first imposed, the result being the development of the industry on a very large scale. It was the same with nails. In 1868 a duty of $30 a ton was imposed on nails. The United States, however, found that the duty of $30 a ton was not sufficient for the English nail was still coming into the country. They therefore increased the duty on nails in 1874 to $80 per ton, less 10 per cent. In 1879 they eliminated the 10 per cent and imposed a flat duty of $80 per ton. The protection was continued until 1894 when the industry had developed to such an extent that the duty on nails was reduced to 25 per cent. The United States was still able to compete with its rivals notwithstanding the reduction, and to-day those same nails are on the free list. It is said, I think on fairly good grounds, that from the steel works in Sydney some 600 different grades of nails went into England during all the years of the war. The United States supplied all its different grades of iron and steel to England, and their nails and their steel products are to be found in the markets of every country in the world. Notwithstanding the fact that they had a high protective tariff, so well established did their steel industry become that they have practically captured the markets of the world, and if they have not done that they are at least able to compete with all other countries at the present time, their products being on the free list.
Now, having that knowledge of the steel industry of the United States, just look at
the present condition of the steel industry here in Canada. We have three large concerns manufacturing steel and steel products in the Dominion, and what are the conditions? In the fiscal year ending March 31, 1920, we imported 1,144,430 tons of iron ore amounting in value to $4,095,839, and for the ten months ending January 1, 1921, we imported 1,302,207 tons having a value of $4,886,942. In agricultural implements we imported from the United States in the fiscal year ending March 31, 1920, $6,792,245 worth; we imported boilers, windmills, pumps, etc., to the value of $22,705,319; of castings we imported $1,958,311 worth; of chains we imported $3,395,496 worth; and so I could go on through all the different grades of steel and steel products imported from the United States alone until I come to the grand total of $178,661,606.
There is your low tariff! There is your hundred and seventy-eight and a half million dollars of Canadian money going into the United States to build up the industries of a foreign and rival nation to the detriment of our own manufacturers, and to the detriment of our own workingmen, who should have earned every dollar of that money. And still you talk free trade. Free trade with whom? Free trade with the United States that has to-day perhaps the highest tariff wall erected against us of any other nation in the world? Trade freely with them? Why, our free trade friend from Victoria and Carleton (Mr. Caldwell) even went so far as to forget his free trade principles and last night talked retaliation. And he was rebuked by the gentleman who sat quite near him, who in bis speech afterwards said retaliation should not be suggested lest it might end in a tariff war. Was that not a very consistent conversation to take place between two paragons of free trade?
Now, Mr. Speaker, I shall pay attention for a few moments to some remarks made this afternoon by my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Crerar). There is an election down in New Brunswick, and my hon. friend referred to it this afternoon.
Who is the Liberal candidate?

They are going to let
that part of it remain in abeyance until the general election. But my hon. friend could not pass over that election without besmirching himself a little more than the man he intended to besmirch. He had to fan as much as he could the smouldering embers of bigotry and race

that have on many occasions, I have no doubt, done yeoman service for gentlemen opposite. He attempted to lead his followers to drink at the polluted stream of religious and racial bigotry and fanaticism; and he would be pleased, I have no doubt, to see them drink at that polluted stream with the same avidity that a buzzard pounces upon his carrion prey.
But, Sir, let me say that he is not altogether alone in that respect, although I had hoped there were none in this House to descend to such arguments. Yet I read in the Montreal Gazette this quotation taken from the nomination day speech at St. Francois du Lac of my hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux). He said:
' When on the 2:8 th you mark your cross, mark it like Laurier would mark his cross if he were voting that day. His shadow is over this assembly, as it hovers over Parliament. He follows our deliberations from the skies and is asking if his compatriots and Canadians of all languages will renew the present regime.
My hon. friend- seems to take on some of Mr. Stead's theories. He is a little spiritualistic-more spiritualistic, I think, than spiritual. But according to the Montreal Star-and, Sir, this is a very delicate subject which I am going to approach, and I wish to deal with it in all reverence and in all respect-my hon. friend from Maisonneuve is reported as having said:
"Meighen is the father of conscription," went on Mr. Lemieux. , "We cannot talk conscription without some emotion. While the Hon. Mr. Ballantyne was trailing his sword in London and Paris, my only son was in the trenches. He is gone; and it seems that I should pay testimony to his memory by working to punish those who brought the atrocity of conscription on our country."
Now, Mr. Speaker, if that is not partisanship gone mad I do not know what is. It is not often, that we find a man who deliberately uses the memory of his departed and lamented offspring to attempt to gain political aggrandizement by playing upon the feelings of an excited nomination day audience and making his departed son the object of commiseration. How much more he would have been admired even by that excited audience had he said to them: "My son was no conscript; he was a volunteer. When his country needed him he sprang to her assistance. He drew his sword in her defence; he bared his breast to the enemies of his country; he in the end made the supreme sacrifice that his country might live." The hon. gentleman might have said to the youngi men of Quebec: "Had you followed his example, 
conscription in this country would have been unnecessary. Had that course been taken by my hon. friend it would have been an honourable course; the memory of his son would be doubly revered and he himself would be doubly respected.
I regret, Mr. Speaker, that the leader of the Opposition is not in the House, for I feel compelled to pay a small amount of attention to him for a few moments. In a previous debate in the session the hon. member for North Cape Breton and Victoria made use of some such expression as this: that one of the many weaknesses of this Government was that it was at war with labour. Well, Mr. Speaker, I do not believe that this Government is so very bellicose as to be at war with labour, or vice versa. If labour is at war with this Government it is doubly bellicose, for certain it is that it has been at war with the leader of the Opposition for many years. Down in our county, some years ago, and also about the same time in Cumberland county, Nova Scotia, while my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition was Minister of Labour, we had a strike in which about 5,000 men were involved. On the morning that the strike broke out the leader of the Opposition, then the Minister of Labour received from M. J. Gillies, M.P.P., of Glace Bay, Nova Scotia, a supporter of the Murray Government at that time, a telegram in which he said:
Five thousand employees Dominion Coal Company on strike here. Situation looks serious. Important that you get here immediately and try to effect a settlement.
How Mr. Macdonald, then the member for Pictou county in this House in the Liberal interest, found out about that is more than I can tell. Suffice it to say that on the same date he wrote a letter to the then Minister of Labour, the present leader of the Opposition, in which he said:
Let me congratulate you upon the fact that you were not troubled with an election and that you have got into the saddle without very much trouble.
It was hinted at that time that the congratulation was not altogether sincere; Mr. Macdonald was very much disappointed, I understand, that he did not get that portfolio. However, the letter went on to say .
I have just teen talking on the phone with our mutual friend Alex. Johnston, and our joint opinion with regard to the situation in Sydney is that at the present stage it iis not wise or prudent for you to come down or take part in the situation. There was a rumour in Sydney that you were to be asked to come

down, and I am writing as a result of my interview with Johnston, to say that I think for the present that you should not come down. We will advise you a little later in the matter.
Now, that appears to me, offhand, to be a little bit mure on the side of Liberalism than on the siue of the labouring men; it was the Liberal party's interests, not the labourihg men's interests, that were being considered, ivir. Alex. Johnston, then the member for South Cape Breton, and Mr. E. M. Macdonald, then the Liberal representative for Pictou county, who at the same time held a retainer from the Dominion Coal Company-these gentlemen went into solemn c.nclave and advised the Minister of Labour as to what it was wise for him to do-no doubt from a political viewpoint. Matters went on; letters passed to and fro, until finally Mr. Macdonald wrote along somewhat-
I presume the hon. member knows that he is reading a letter which was stolen-taken from the files.
I do not care whether it was stolen or not.
I believe that.
I did not steal it. My hon. friend car see that I am reading from Hansard, not from a letter at all.
My hon. friend is quite welcome to all the capital he can make of it.

Order.
Mr. BUTTS [DOT] Whether I am welcome or not, I am going to have it. Mr. Macdonald then writes to the Minister of Labour, the present leader of the Opposition, as follows:
The strike situation in Nova Scotia has been summarized in this way, that in Inverness the strike practically does not exist. There are some men who are not working, but these men are not necessary to the adequate operation of the mines. In the Dominion Coal Company's works, from which I have just returned, the company are rapidly increasing their output, and the men are only being kept out on strike, at least a great portion of them, by the actual stories which the resources of the United Mine Workers' people supply to them, of the fact that the company are going to settle and various reasons are given for this from week to week. I do not doubt at all that the company will be successful there, and there may be a break very shortly.
There is no doubt in the world that Mr. Macdonald took it for granted that there was reassuring evidence that the company was going to win out and that the labouring men were going to be defeated in the strike. The letter continues:
I think that the men will eventually realize that the company will not on any terms settle their compromise. The Springhill situation is one I am not advised about and is really very serious. The situation at Inverness and the action of the United Mine Workers is a direct and absolute defiance of the provisions of the Conciliation Act, and I think it would be a great mistake if the department itself-not the company or any outside party or person-did not proceed against the United Mine Workers people who came out on strike in disregard of that Act. I notice by the press that inquiries are being made by the department with reference to the circumstances, and I am quite sure that you will find the facts to be that the strike is one which is in contravention to the Act. And can assure you of my fullest support in so doing if you should arrange to have these proceedings initiated. It seems to me that the effect of the department proceeding against this infraction of their own law would be a very good move in Nova Scotia.
He continues:
At the present time public opinion is strongly against the strikers and against every one who is connected with them, and there is no question about their desire to have the matter speedily dealt with by a strong hand. In the event of your taking any proceedings, I would suggest that the matter be put in the hands of some recognized lawyer of ability, such as Mr. Roscoe, of Kentville, who has been acting for the Militia Department and making some investigations in that matter. I should be very glad to hear from you in regard to this matter.
It would appear from the entire correspondence-it is rather lengthy, and I do not wish to weary the House by reading it- that the Labour Department in that strike was being advised by the solicitor of the Dominion Coal Company, Mr. E. M. Macdonald, who was then a member of Parliament, representing Pictou county in this House. There were prosecutions down there. But let me call this one fact-and it is a fact-to the attention of the House. Not only were there prosecutions; but before there was any overt act, before there was anything that showed sign or semblance of disorder in the entire community, a large detachment of soldiers landed there. When I say this, I wish to assure the House that prior to the time that those soldiers arrived, there was no such thing as a disturbance or a violation of the law in any one particular case. Shortly after the soldiers arrived there, the men were holding a procession, not a military parade or anything like tb't. They carried no arms; they were peaceful, peaceable, law-abiding men; they had shown no sign of attempting to disturb the serenity of the entire com-

munity; but while is that state of mind those men were parading, a line was drawn and a machine gun was set up before Bridgeport Catholic church and the men were ordered not to pass that line on peril of being fired upon. That was done while the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) was Minister of Labour. Do you wonder then that I say that the men are not sufficiently bellicose to be at war with this Government because they are already at war with the Opposition and the leaders of the Opposition. They may forgive those things; they are a forgiving people, but they have good memories. I feel very much inclined to believe that before the Opposition in this House can hold out any hopes of winning seats in Cape Breton county at least, they will have to swap horses, even if they do that when crossing the stream.
I have finished pretty nearly all that I intended to say, and the night is getting late. I have only this to say, in conclusion, that I notice down in the "Annex" they seem to be a little bit stronger than those hon. gentlemen in the official Opposition, and it seems strange to me how they are going to affect .a union, or anything approaching the marital tie. You have to raise your tariff before you can come up to those protectionists opposite or you have to lure them away with your free-trade theories, and I cannot very well understand how you are going to carry on the negotiations when I consider the fact that not a man in the "Annex" can talk French. I would ask you gentlemen of the "Annex" down there to consider these matters and to see if it is not possible for you-

speechtext: I must remind the hon. member that he should address the Chair.

I beg your pardon, Sir- to see if it is not possible for them to take the advice of the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) the other evening, when he told them to throw away the mask, to come out into the open and to form the union in order that we might possibly have a little bit of jollification before we have an election.
On motion of Mr. Proulx (Prescott) the debate was adjourned.
